title: Practical Skills Academy
description: Real-life skills for everyday independence, safety, and wellbeing — progressing from beginner to advanced.

skills.title: Wash Hands Before Cooking
skills.description: Always wash hands with soap and water for 20 seconds before touching food.
skills.why: Prevents germs from spreading to food and people.

skills.title: Make a Simple Sandwich
skills.description: Spread butter on two bread slices. Add filling (cheese, jam, or salad). Press together and cut diagonally.
skills.why: Independence skill — being able to prepare your own snack.

skills.title: Pour a Safe Drink
skills.description: Use both hands to hold a jug or bottle. Pour slowly over the sink first to practise control.

quiz.question: How long should you wash your hands before cooking?
What is the safest way to hold a knife when cutting?
options: With a 'claw' grip on the food

skills.title: Boil Pasta Safely
skills.description: Fill pot with water, add salt, bring to boil. Add pasta, stir. Cook per packet instructions. Drain carefully with adult supervision for hot water.
skills.why: Core cooking skill; teaches heat safety.

skills.title: Scrambled Eggs
skills.description: Crack 2 eggs into a bowl, beat with fork. Add pinch of salt. Cook in buttered pan on medium heat, stirring gently until just set.

skills.title: Read and Follow a Recipe
skills.description: Gather all ingredients first (mise en place). Read all steps before starting. Measure accurately. Follow steps in order.
skills.why: Planning and literacy skills applied to cooking.

quiz.question: What does 'mise en place' mean?
options: Everything in its place — ingredients prepared before cooking

quiz.question: Why do we add salt to pasta water?
options: For flavour and to season the pasta

skills.title: Plan a Weekly Menu
skills.description: Plan 7 dinners considering nutrition (proteins, vegetables, carbs), budget, and variety. Write a shopping list organised by supermarket section.

skills.title: Safe Knife Skills
skills.description: Learn the claw grip, bridge grip, and rocking motion. Keep knives sharp — dull knives slip. Always cut away from your body.
skills.why: Safety and efficiency in the kitchen.

skills.title: Bake a Simple Loaf
skills.description: Mix 500g flour, 7g yeast, 1 tsp salt, 300ml warm water. Knead 10 min, rest 1 hour, shape, prove 30 min, bake 200°C for 30 min.
skills.why: Teaches chemistry of yeast, patience, and planning.

quiz.question: What is the correct internal temperature for cooked chicken?
What does 'sauté' mean?
options: Cook in a small amount of oil over high heat while stirring

skills.title: Kitchen Safety
skills.explanation: Learn how to stay safe while cooking.
steps: Wash your hands before cooking.
Keep knives pointed down.
Never leave hot pans unattended.
Use oven gloves when handling hot items.
Keep a clean workspace.
skills.tip: Always ask an adult before using the oven or hob.

quiz.question: What should you do before handling food?
Why should you use oven gloves?
options: To protect your hands from heat

skills.title: Knife Skills
skills.explanation: Use a knife safely and effectively.
steps: Choose the right knife for the job.
Use a chopping board.
Curl your fingers under (the 'claw' grip).
Cut slowly and steadily.
Never pass a knife blade-first.
skills.tip: A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one — ask an adult to check.

skills.title: Boiling and Simmering
skills.explanation: Learn to cook with water on the hob.
steps: Fill a pot with cold water and place on the hob.
Turn the heat to high to bring to a boil.
Add food once boiling.
Reduce heat to simmer — small gentle bubbles.
Test food is cooked through before serving.
skills.tip: Salt the water for pasta and vegetables to add flavour.

quiz.question: When do you add pasta to water?

skills.title: Baking Basics
steps: Read the recipe fully before starting.
Measure all ingredients accurately.
Preheat the oven to the correct temperature.
Mix dry and wet ingredients separately then combine.
Test baked goods with a skewer — it should come out clean.
skills.tip: Room-temperature butter creams more easily than cold butter.

quiz.question: Why preheat the oven?
options: So food cooks evenly from the start

quiz.question: How do you test if a cake is baked?
options: Insert a skewer — clean means done

skills.title: Simple Recipes
skills.explanation: Cook three easy meals from scratch.
steps: Scrambled eggs: whisk eggs, cook gently in butter, stir constantly.
Pasta with tomato sauce: boil pasta, fry garlic, add tinned tomatoes, season.
Vegetable stir-fry: chop veg, heat oil, add hard veg first then soft veg, add soy sauce.
skills.tip: Taste as you cook and adjust seasoning gradually.

quiz.question: Which vegetables go into the pan first in a stir-fry?
options: Hard ones like carrot and broccoli

modules.title: Kitchen Safety Basics
modules.description: Learn the basic rules to stay safe in the kitchen.
learning_objectives: Identify kitchen hazards
Know when to ask an adult for help
steps: Learn about hot surfaces and sharp objects
Understand why we wash hands before cooking
Practice turning appliances off
Learn proper knife safety (blunt/child knives only)
modules.hands_on_activity: Wash vegetables safely and arrange them on a plate without any cutting.

quiz.q: What should you do before handling food?
quiz.a: Wash your hands

quiz.q: What should you do with hot pots?
quiz.a: Ask an adult for help

modules.pro_tip: Always ask an adult before using the stove or oven.
modules.lesson_text:
This lesson covers Kitchen Safety Basics in depth. Learn the basic rules to stay safe in the kitchen. Rather than treating it as a trick to memorise, the goal here is genuine competence: understanding the reasoning behind each step well enough that you could explain it to someone else, adapt it when conditions change, and recognise when something is going wrong early enough to correct it.

It is worth pausing on why this lesson matters before diving in. Competence at a practical skill is not just about the skill itself; it changes how you approach unfamiliar problems generally. When you have genuinely mastered even one hands-on skill -- taken it from clumsy first attempts to smooth, reliable execution -- you know from experience that difficulty is temporary and that methodical practice works. That confidence, built on real evidence rather than positive thinking, is one of the most valuable things any learner can own, and every lesson in this pathway is another chance to reinforce it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Identify kitchen hazards; Know when to ask an adult for help. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: child-safe knife, cutting board, hand soap. Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

The heart of the lesson is the following sequence. Read all the steps once before performing any of them, so you know where each one is heading. Step 1: Learn about hot surfaces and sharp objects. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing. Step 2: Understand why we wash hands before cooking. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence. Step 3: Practice turning appliances off. There is no prize for hurrying this step -- accuracy first, then rhythm, then speed, in that order. Step 4: Learn proper knife safety (blunt/child knives only). Once this feels comfortable, try to notice what changed compared with your first attempt; that awareness is itself a skill and accelerates everything that follows.

Watch for the classic failure modes. Overconfidence after early success leads people to add speed or difficulty before the foundation is stable, and progress collapses. Frustration after early failure leads people to conclude they lack talent, when in fact almost every stumble at this stage is simply a step being taken too fast or out of order. And inconsistency -- practising intensely once and then not at all for weeks -- wastes most of the effort invested, because skills consolidate through repetition spaced over time. Steady, modest, correct practice beats occasional heroic effort by a wide margin.

A note on safety and good judgement: Always ask an adult before using the stove or oven. Build this into how you practise from the very first session, because safety habits are learned exactly the way every other habit is learned -- through repetition -- and it is far easier to build the careful version now than to retrofit it later.

Your practice assignment: Wash vegetables safely and arrange them on a plate without any cutting. After each session, spend one minute on deliberate review: what went well, what broke down, and what single thing you will focus on next time. This tiny habit -- professionals call it a debrief -- is the highest-leverage minute in the entire practice session, because it converts experience into insight while the details are still fresh.

Test yourself: What should you do before handling food? If your answer matches 'Wash your hands' and, more importantly, you can explain why, you are ready to continue. If not, revisit the steps above -- the gap is almost always in one specific step, and finding it now is cheap compared with finding it later.

When you feel ready to advance, resist the urge to jump to something entirely new. The efficient path is to deepen this skill first: perform it more smoothly, from memory, under less forgiving conditions, or while explaining it aloud to someone else. Teaching, even informally, is the fastest known test of real understanding -- gaps that hide during solo practice become obvious the moment you try to explain a step. When you can teach this lesson convincingly, you have genuinely learned it.

Remember where this sits in the wider Cooking & Nutrition pathway: the lessons before it built the context this one relies on, and the lessons after it will assume the ability you are building now. If any prerequisite feels shaky, a quick review before the next session is cheap insurance.

To close: aim for progress, not perfection. The standard to hold yourself to is simple -- a little more correct, a little more confident, and a little more consistent than last session. Skills built that way do not evaporate under stress, because they were never memorised tricks in the first place; they were understood. Keep the steps above where you can revisit them, log your practice, respect the safety guidance, and this skill will move steadily from something you are learning to something you simply have.

modules.title: Fruit Salad & Simple Snacks

modules.title: Baking Cookies

Follow a recipe
Understand baking times and temperatures
steps: Pre-heat oven (adult)

modules.title: Balanced Meals & Nutrition
modules.description: Plan and prepare a nutritionally balanced meal.
learning_objectives: Identify the five food groups
Plan a balanced plate
Cook a simple balanced meal
steps: Study the food plate diagram
Plan a meal with protein, carbs, vegetables, fruit
Prepare a simple pasta dish with vegetables
Assess nutritional value
modules.hands_on_activity: Cook a simple vegetable pasta and annotate which food groups are present.

modules.title: Boiling and Blanching Vegetables
modules.description: Boiling cooks food fully submerged in rapidly bubbling water, while blanching is a brief boil followed by an ice water bath to stop cooking and preserve color and crunch. This lesson covers both techniques for vegetables like green beans and broccoli.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Boiling and Blanching Vegetables
Boiling cooks food fully submerged in rapidly bubbling water, while blanching is a brief boil followed by an ice water bath to stop cooking and preserve color and crunch.
steps: Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil

Drain thoroughly before serving or storing
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Boiling and Blanching Vegetables" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is blanched food shocked in ice water immediately after boiling?

modules.title: Roasting Vegetables in the Oven
modules.description: Roasting uses dry oven heat to caramelize the natural sugars in vegetables, creating deep flavor and crisp edges. This lesson covers proper oven temperature, spacing, and oil coating for even roasting.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Roasting Vegetables in the Oven
Roasting uses dry oven heat to caramelize the natural sugars in vegetables, creating deep flavor and crisp edges.
steps: Preheat the oven to a high roasting temperature, around 200-220C (400-425F)
Toss vegetables in oil, salt, and pepper until evenly coated
Spread in a single layer with space between pieces, not overlapping
Roast until edges are golden brown, flipping halfway through
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Roasting Vegetables in the Oven" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why should roasted vegetables be spread out with space between them?

modules.pro_tip: Cut vegetables to a uniform size so they all finish roasting at the same time.

modules.title: Marinating for Flavor and Tenderness
modules.description: Marinades combine acid, oil, and seasonings to add flavor and, in some cases, tenderize meat before cooking. This lesson covers safe marinating times and food-safety practices like never reusing raw marinade as a sauce.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Marinating for Flavor and Tenderness
Marinades combine acid, oil, and seasonings to add flavor and, in some cases, tenderize meat before cooking.
steps: Combine acid, oil, and seasonings in a bowl or bag
Add the food and ensure it's fully coated
Refrigerate for the appropriate time, from 30 minutes for fish to several hours for tougher meat
Discard used marinade or boil it thoroughly before using it as a sauce
materials_needed: Acid such as citrus juice or vinegar
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Marinating for Flavor and Tenderness" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is it unsafe to use raw meat marinade as a serving sauce without cooking it?

Marinades combine acid, oil, and seasonings to add flavor and, in some cases, tenderize meat before cooking. This lesson covers safe marinating times and food-safety practices like never reusing raw marinade as a sauce. This lesson walks through the skill from first principles: what it is, why it matters, what you need before you begin, how to work through it step by step, the mistakes that most commonly trip up beginners, and how to practise it until it becomes reliable under real conditions rather than something you can only do on a good day.

Before touching the steps, it helps to understand why this skill earns a place in the curriculum. Skills like this one compound: each hour of correct, focused practice makes the next hour more productive, and the habits you build here -- preparing properly, working in the right order, checking your results -- transfer directly to every other skill in this pathway. Learners who rush past the fundamentals usually have to come back and relearn them later, at greater cost. Taking the time to get the basic pattern right the first time is the single most efficient thing you can do.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: Marinating for Flavor and Tenderness; Marinades combine acid, oil, and seasonings to add flavor and, in some cases, tenderize meat before cooking. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: Acid such as citrus juice or vinegar, Oil, Herbs and spices, Sealable bag or container. Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

Now work through the core sequence. Take each step slowly the first several times; speed comes later, and comes faster if you don't chase it early. Step 1: Combine acid, oil, and seasonings in a bowl or bag. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly. Step 2: Add the food and ensure it's fully coated. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing. Step 3: Refrigerate for the appropriate time, from 30 minutes for fish to several hours for tougher meat. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence. Step 4: Discard used marinade or boil it thoroughly before using it as a sauce. There is no prize for hurrying this step -- accuracy first, then rhythm, then speed, in that order.

Watch for the classic failure modes. Overconfidence after early success leads people to add speed or difficulty before the foundation is stable, and progress collapses. Frustration after early failure leads people to conclude they lack talent, when in fact almost every stumble at this stage is simply a step being taken too fast or out of order. And inconsistency -- practising intensely once and then not at all for weeks -- wastes most of the effort invested, because skills consolidate through repetition spaced over time. Steady, modest, correct practice beats occasional heroic effort by a wide margin.

A note on safety and good judgement: Never marinate for too long, since strong acid can make delicate proteins like fish or shrimp mushy. Build this into how you practise from the very first session, because safety habits are learned exactly the way every other habit is learned -- through repetition -- and it is far easier to build the careful version now than to retrofit it later.

Your practice assignment: Practice "Marinating for Flavor and Tenderness" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed. After each session, spend one minute on deliberate review: what went well, what broke down, and what single thing you will focus on next time. This tiny habit -- professionals call it a debrief -- is the highest-leverage minute in the entire practice session, because it converts experience into insight while the details are still fresh.

Test yourself: Why is it unsafe to use raw meat marinade as a serving sauce without cooking it? If your answer matches 'It contains raw juices that may carry bacteria, so it must be boiled first to be safe' and, more importantly, you can explain why, you are ready to continue. If not, revisit the steps above -- the gap is almost always in one specific step, and finding it now is cheap compared with finding it later.

When you feel ready to advance, resist the urge to jump to something entirely new. The efficient path is to deepen this skill first: perform it more smoothly, from memory, under less forgiving conditions, or while explaining it aloud to someone else. Teaching, even informally, is the fastest known test of real understanding -- gaps that hide during solo practice become obvious the moment you try to explain a step. When you can teach this lesson convincingly, you have genuinely learned it.

Remember where this sits in the wider Cooking & Nutrition pathway: the lessons before it built the context this one relies on, and the lessons after it will assume the ability you are building now. If any prerequisite feels shaky, a quick review before the next session is cheap insurance.

To close: aim for progress, not perfection. The standard to hold yourself to is simple -- a little more correct, a little more confident, and a little more consistent than last session. Skills built that way do not evaporate under stress, because they were never memorised tricks in the first place; they were understood. modules.title: Knife Skills: Basic Cuts (Dice and Slice)
modules.description: Consistent knife cuts ensure even cooking and professional presentation. This lesson introduces the large dice, medium dice, and small dice, along with basic slicing technique using the claw grip learned earlier.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Knife Skills: Basic Cuts (Dice and Slice)
Consistent knife cuts ensure even cooking and professional presentation.
steps: Square off the vegetable by trimming rounded edges for stability
Cut the vegetable into even planks, then into even sticks
Line up the sticks and cut crosswise into cubes of the desired size
Keep cube sizes consistent within a batch, roughly 2cm for large dice, 1cm for medium, 0.5cm for small
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Knife Skills: Basic Cuts (Dice and Slice)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is squaring off a vegetable's edges the first step in dicing?
quiz.a: It creates flat, stable surfaces so the vegetable won't roll or slip while being cut

modules.pro_tip: Keep the knife tip anchored on the board and use a rocking motion for faster, safer dicing.

modules.title: Julienne and Batonnet Cuts
modules.description: Julienne and batonnet are matchstick-style cuts used in stir-fries, garnishes, and French cuisine; batonnet is thicker (about 6mm x 6mm x 6cm) while julienne is finer (about 3mm x 3mm x 5cm). This lesson builds precision knife control for uniform strips.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Julienne and Batonnet Cuts
Julienne and batonnet are matchstick-style cuts used in stir-fries, garnishes, and French cuisine; batonnet is thicker (about 6mm x 6mm x 6cm) while julienne is finer (about 3mm x 3mm x 5cm).
steps: Trim the vegetable into a rectangular block by squaring the sides
Slice the block lengthwise into even planks about 3-6mm thick
Stack the planks and cut lengthwise into even strips
For julienne, cut strips thinner than batonnet, roughly matchstick width
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Julienne and Batonnet Cuts" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is the main size difference between a batonnet and a julienne cut?
quiz.a: Batonnet is a thicker matchstick cut (about 6mm square) while julienne is thinner (about 3mm square)

modules.pro_tip: Stack only a few plank slices at a time so the knife can cut cleanly through all layers.

modules.title: Brunoise and Fine Dice
modules.description: Brunoise is a very fine dice, about 3mm cubes, made by first cutting a julienne and then dicing it crosswise; it's used for garnishes and delicate sauces like a classic tomato brunoise. This lesson refines precision cutting for professional presentation.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Brunoise and Fine Dice
Brunoise is a very fine dice, about 3mm cubes, made by first cutting a julienne and then dicing it crosswise; it's used for garnishes and delicate sauces like a classic tomato brunoise.
steps: Cut the vegetable into a fine julienne (about 3mm strips) first
Gather the julienne strips together, keeping them aligned
Cut crosswise at 3mm intervals to create tiny, even cubes
Work slowly since brunoise prioritizes precision over speed
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Brunoise and Fine Dice" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What two steps combine to create a brunoise cut?
quiz.a: Cutting a fine julienne first, then dicing that julienne crosswise into tiny cubes

modules.pro_tip: Keep julienne strips tightly aligned before the crosswise cut so the final brunoise cubes stay uniform.

modules.title: Chiffonade for Leafy Herbs and Greens
modules.description: Chiffonade is a technique for cutting leafy herbs like basil or leafy greens into thin ribbons by rolling and slicing. This lesson teaches how to garnish and finish dishes with fine, elegant strips of herbs without bruising them.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Chiffonade for Leafy Herbs and Greens
Chiffonade is a technique for cutting leafy herbs like basil or leafy greens into thin ribbons by rolling and slicing.
steps: Stack several leaves of similar size on top of each other
Roll the stack tightly into a cigar shape
Slice thinly crosswise with a sharp knife to create thin ribbons
Fluff the ribbons apart gently before sprinkling over the dish
materials_needed: Basil leaves or other leafy herbs
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Chiffonade for Leafy Herbs and Greens" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is a very sharp knife important for chiffonade?
quiz.a: A dull knife bruises and tears delicate leaves instead of slicing them cleanly, causing browning

modules.pro_tip: Cut chiffonade just before serving since cut herbs bruise and darken quickly once exposed to air.

modules.title: Braising Tougher Cuts of Meat

learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Braising Tougher Cuts of Meat

materials_needed: Dutch oven or heavy pot with lid

modules.description: Steaming cooks food with hot vapor rather than submerging it in water, preserving more nutrients, color, and delicate texture, common in Chinese dim sum and many vegetable preparations. This lesson covers steamer setup and timing.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Steaming for Delicate Flavors and Nutrients
Steaming cooks food with hot vapor rather than submerging it in water, preserving more nutrients, color, and delicate texture, common in Chinese dim sum and many vegetable preparations.
steps: Fill the pot with a few centimeters of water, below the level of the steamer basket
Bring the water to a boil so steam builds up
Place food in the steamer basket, arranged with space for steam to circulate
Cover tightly and steam until cooked through, checking water level for longer cooks
materials_needed: Food to steam (fish, dumplings, or vegetables)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Steaming for Delicate Flavors and Nutrients" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does steaming preserve nutrients better than boiling?

learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Deep Frying Technique and Safety
Deep frying submerges food in hot oil, typically 160-190C (325-375F), to create a crisp exterior quickly while sealing in moisture, as used for French fries, tempura, and fried chicken.
steps: Heat oil to the target temperature, checking with a thermometer
Pat food dry and coat as the recipe requires (batter, breading, or plain)
Lower food into the oil gently and away from you to avoid splashing
Fry in small batches so the oil temperature doesn't drop too much, then drain on paper towels
materials_needed: Deep, heavy pot or deep fryer
Neutral oil with a high smoke point
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Deep Frying Technique and Safety" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is frying in small batches important?

modules.title: Stir-Frying and Wok Technique
modules.description: Stir-frying is a fast, high-heat Chinese technique using a wok to cook small, evenly cut pieces of food while tossing constantly, sealing in flavor and keeping vegetables crisp, as in classic beef and broccoli. This lesson introduces wok hei and proper wok heat management.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Stir-Frying and Wok Technique

Stir-frying is a fast, high-heat Chinese technique using a wok to cook small, evenly cut pieces of food while tossing constantly, sealing in flavor and keeping vegetables crisp, as in classic beef and broccoli.
steps: Prep and cut all ingredients before turning on the heat, since stir-frying moves fast
Heat the wok until very hot, then add oil and swirl to coat the sides
Add aromatics briefly, then proteins, then vegetables in order of cooking time needed
Toss and stir constantly over high heat, adding sauce at the end to coat everything
materials_needed: Pre-cut, uniform ingredients (mise en place is essential)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Stir-Frying and Wok Technique" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why must all ingredients be prepped before you start stir-frying?

modules.pro_tip: Keep the wok and oil very hot before adding food to achieve 'wok hei,' the smoky charred flavor of great stir-fry.

modules.title: BBQ and Grilling Fundamentals
modules.description: Grilling cooks food directly over high heat for quick charring, while barbecue (BBQ) traditionally refers to slow, indirect cooking with smoke over low heat for hours, as with American pulled pork or brisket. This lesson distinguishes direct versus indirect heat zones.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: BBQ and Grilling Fundamentals

Grilling cooks food directly over high heat for quick charring, while barbecue (BBQ) traditionally refers to slow, indirect cooking with smoke over low heat for hours, as with American pulled pork or brisket.
steps: Set up two heat zones: direct high heat and an indirect cooler zone
Sear food over direct heat first for color and grill marks
Move food to the indirect zone to finish cooking through without burning
Use a meat thermometer to confirm safe internal temperatures rather than guessing by time
materials_needed: Charcoal or wood chips if smoking
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "BBQ and Grilling Fundamentals" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is the difference between grilling and traditional barbecue?

modules.pro_tip: Let grilled meat rest for several minutes after cooking so its juices redistribute instead of spilling out when cut.

modules.title: Smoking Meat Low and Slow
modules.description: Smoking uses indirect heat and wood smoke over many hours (often 4-14+ hours) to tenderize tough cuts and infuse deep flavor, as with Texas-style brisket or Southern pulled pork shoulder. This lesson covers temperature control and the 'stall' phenomenon.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Smoking Meat Low and Slow
Smoking uses indirect heat and wood smoke over many hours (often 4-14+ hours) to tenderize tough cuts and infuse deep flavor, as with Texas-style brisket or Southern pulled pork shoulder.
steps: Maintain a steady low temperature, typically 107-135C (225-275F), throughout the cook
Add wood chunks or chips periodically for consistent smoke, not constant billowing smoke
Expect the internal temperature to plateau or 'stall' partway through; this is normal
Cook until the meat reaches a tender internal temperature, often 93-96C (200-205F) for brisket, then rest wrapped
materials_needed: Smoker or grill set up for indirect heat
Wood chips or chunks (hickory, oak, applewood)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Smoking Meat Low and Slow" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is 'the stall' in smoking, and how should you respond to it?
quiz.a: A period where the meat's internal temperature plateaus for hours due to evaporative cooling; keep smoking patiently, don't raise heat drastically

modules.pro_tip: Wrap the meat in butcher paper or foil during the stall (the 'Texas crutch') to push through the plateau faster.

modules.title: Making Fresh Pasta by Hand
modules.description: Fresh Italian pasta is traditionally made from flour and eggs, kneaded into a smooth dough, rested, then rolled thin and cut, as in classic fettuccine or tagliatelle. This lesson covers dough hydration, kneading, and resting.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Making Fresh Pasta by Hand
Fresh Italian pasta is traditionally made from flour and eggs, kneaded into a smooth dough, rested, then rolled thin and cut, as in classic fettuccine or tagliatelle.
steps: Mound flour on a work surface, make a well, and crack eggs into the center

modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Making Fresh Pasta by Hand" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

modules.title: Classic Italian: Risotto Technique
modules.description: Risotto is a creamy Northern Italian rice dish made by slowly adding warm broth to arborio or carnaroli rice while stirring constantly, releasing starch for its signature creaminess, as in risotto alla Milanese with saffron. This lesson covers the incremental-liquid technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Classic Italian: Risotto Technique

Risotto is a creamy Northern Italian rice dish made by slowly adding warm broth to arborio or carnaroli rice while stirring constantly, releasing starch for its signature creaminess, as in risotto alla Milanese with saffron.
steps: Toast the rice briefly in butter until edges turn slightly translucent
Add a splash of wine and let it absorb, stirring
Add warm broth one ladle at a time, stirring frequently and waiting for each addition to absorb
Finish off heat by stirring in butter and parmesan for a creamy texture (mantecatura)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Classic Italian: Risotto Technique" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is broth added gradually rather than all at once in risotto?
quiz.a: Slow addition with constant stirring releases the rice's starch gradually, creating risotto's characteristic creaminess

modules.pro_tip: Keep the broth warm on a nearby burner, since adding cold broth shocks the rice and slows even cooking.

modules.title: French Technique: Sauteing and the Five Mother Sauces
modules.description: Classical French cuisine is built on five 'mother sauces' -- bechamel, veloute, espagnole, tomato, and hollandaise -- from which many smaller sauces derive. This lesson introduces bechamel, a roux-based white sauce, as a foundation.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: French Technique: Sauteing and the Five Mother Sauces
Classical French cuisine is built on five 'mother sauces' -- bechamel, veloute, espagnole, tomato, and hollandaise -- from which many smaller sauces derive.
steps: Melt butter in a saucepan and whisk in an equal amount of flour to form a roux
Cook the roux for 1-2 minutes to remove the raw flour taste, without browning it
Gradually whisk in warm milk, a little at a time, to avoid lumps
Simmer, whisking, until thickened, then season with salt, pepper, and nutmeg
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "French Technique: Sauteing and the Five Mother Sauces" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is a roux, and what is its purpose in bechamel sauce?
quiz.a: A roux is equal parts fat and flour cooked together, used as a thickening base for sauces like bechamel

modules.pro_tip: Whisk in warm milk rather than cold milk to help the sauce thicken smoothly without lumps.

modules.title: French Classic: Coq au Vin
modules.description: Coq au vin is a traditional French braise of chicken slowly cooked in red wine with mushrooms, pearl onions, and bacon (lardons), showcasing braising technique applied to poultry. This lesson walks through the full classic preparation.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: French Classic: Coq au Vin
Coq au vin is a traditional French braise of chicken slowly cooked in red wine with mushrooms, pearl onions, and bacon (lardons), showcasing braising technique applied to poultry.
steps: Render bacon lardons in a Dutch oven, then remove and set aside
Sear chicken pieces in the rendered fat until browned
Saute mushrooms and onions, then return chicken and bacon and add red wine to partially cover
Cover and braise low and slow until the chicken is tender, then reduce the sauce
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "French Classic: Coq au Vin" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What role does the red wine play in coq au vin?
quiz.a: It's the primary braising liquid, tenderizing the chicken while infusing deep, rich flavor into the sauce

modules.pro_tip: Choose a decent-quality red wine you'd actually drink, since a poor wine's flavor concentrates and shows through in the sauce.

modules.title: Chinese Technique: Velveting Meat
modules.description: Velveting is a Chinese technique of coating thin-sliced meat in a mixture of egg white, cornstarch, and sometimes rice wine, then briefly blanching or oil-poaching it before stir-frying, which keeps the meat exceptionally tender and silky. Velveting is a Chinese technique of coating thin-sliced meat in a mixture of egg white, cornstarch, and sometimes rice wine, then briefly blanching or oil-poaching it before stir-frying, which keeps the meat exceptionally tender and silky.
steps: Slice meat thinly against the grain for tenderness
Mix with egg white, cornstarch, and a splash of rice wine; marinate 15-30 minutes
Briefly blanch the coated meat in warm oil or simmering water until just opaque
Drain and add to the stir-fry near the end of cooking to finish
materials_needed: Thinly sliced chicken, beef, or shrimp

modules.title: Chinese Classic: Kung Pao Chicken
modules.description: Kung Pao chicken is a Sichuan stir-fry combining diced chicken, peanuts, and dried chilies in a savory-sweet-tangy sauce of soy sauce, vinegar, and sugar, showcasing the balance of Sichuan flavors and proper wok stir-frying. This lesson walks through the full dish.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Chinese Classic: Kung Pao Chicken

Kung Pao chicken is a Sichuan stir-fry combining diced chicken, peanuts, and dried chilies in a savory-sweet-tangy sauce of soy sauce, vinegar, and sugar, showcasing the balance of Sichuan flavors and proper wok stir-frying.
steps: Velvet or marinate the diced chicken briefly in soy sauce and cornstarch
Stir-fry dried chilies and Sichuan peppercorns in hot oil until fragrant, careful not to burn them
Add chicken and stir-fry until just cooked through
Add the mixed sauce and peanuts, tossing quickly until the sauce thickens and coats everything
materials_needed: Dried red chilies and Sichuan peppercorns
Soy sauce, vinegar, sugar, cornstarch for sauce
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Chinese Classic: Kung Pao Chicken" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What flavor profile is Kung Pao chicken known for balancing?
quiz.a: A savory, sweet, tangy, and spicy balance, along with the numbing 'mala' sensation from Sichuan peppercorns

modules.pro_tip: Toast dried chilies and peppercorns briefly in oil to release their aroma, but pull them before they blacken and turn bitter.

modules.title: Japanese Technique: Dashi and Umami Base
modules.description: Dashi is a foundational Japanese stock made from kombu (dried kelp) and katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes), delivering deep umami flavor used in miso soup, noodle broths, and countless dishes. This lesson teaches the simple two-ingredient brewing method.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Japanese Technique: Dashi and Umami Base
Dashi is a foundational Japanese stock made from kombu (dried kelp) and katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes), delivering deep umami flavor used in miso soup, noodle broths, and countless dishes.
steps: Soak kombu in cold water for 30 minutes or longer to draw out flavor
Slowly heat the water almost to a boil, then remove the kombu just before boiling
Add bonito flakes and let steep briefly off heat, about 1-2 minutes, without stirring
Strain through a fine strainer or cloth to yield clear dashi
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Japanese Technique: Dashi and Umami Base" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is the kombu removed just before the water boils?
quiz.a: Boiling kombu releases bitterness and a slimy texture, so it's pulled right before the boiling point

modules.pro_tip: Let bonito flakes settle to the bottom of the pot on their own rather than stirring, for a clear, clean-tasting dashi.

modules.title: Japanese Classic: Chicken Teriyaki and Glazing
modules.description: Teriyaki is a Japanese cooking technique where food is grilled or pan-fried and coated in a glaze of soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar, reduced until glossy and sticky, as in classic teriyaki chicken. This lesson covers building and applying a proper glaze.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Japanese Classic: Chicken Teriyaki and Glazing

Teriyaki is a Japanese cooking technique where food is grilled or pan-fried and coated in a glaze of soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar, reduced until glossy and sticky, as in classic teriyaki chicken.
steps: Combine soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar in a saucepan and simmer until slightly thickened
Pan-sear the chicken skin-side down until browned and mostly cooked through
Pour off excess fat, then add the teriyaki sauce to the pan
Simmer and baste the chicken repeatedly until the sauce reduces to a glossy glaze that coats it
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Japanese Classic: Chicken Teriyaki and Glazing" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What are the four core ingredients of a classic teriyaki glaze?
quiz.a: Soy sauce, mirin, sake, and sugar

modules.pro_tip: Baste the chicken continuously in the reducing sauce so the glaze builds up in even, glossy layers.

modules.title: Indian Classic: Butter Chicken (Murgh Makhani)

modules.title: Mexican Technique: Making a Proper Salsa and Roasting Chiles
modules.description: Roasting tomatoes, chiles, and other aromatics on a comal or under a broiler before blending is a foundational Mexican technique that deepens flavor with smoky char, used in salsas like salsa roja. This lesson covers the char-then-blend method.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Mexican Technique: Making a Proper Salsa and Roasting Chiles

Blend everything together with salt and a splash of water to the desired consistency

modules.title: Mexican Classic: Tacos al Pastor
modules.description: Tacos al pastor feature pork marinated in a blend of dried chiles, pineapple, and spices, traditionally cooked on a vertical spit (trompo) influenced by Lebanese shawarma, then sliced thin and served on small tortillas with pineapple, onion, and cilantro. Sear the marinated pork in a very hot skillet in batches until charred and cooked through
Chop finely and serve on warmed tortillas with diced pineapple, onion, and cilantro

modules.title: Thai Classic: Green Curry (Gaeng Keow Wan)
modules.description: Thai green curry combines a pounded paste of green chilies, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste with coconut milk, showcasing how a curry paste is bloomed in coconut cream before liquid is added. This lesson covers the paste-blooming technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Thai Classic: Green Curry (Gaeng Keow Wan)
Thai green curry combines a pounded paste of green chilies, lemongrass, galangal, and shrimp paste with coconut milk, showcasing how a curry paste is bloomed in coconut cream before liquid is added.
steps: Simmer the thick cream that rises to the top of unshaken coconut milk until the oil separates
Add curry paste to the separated coconut cream and fry until deeply fragrant
Add protein and cook briefly, then pour in remaining coconut milk
Add vegetables and simmer until cooked, finishing with Thai basil leaves
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Thai Classic: Green Curry (Gaeng Keow Wan)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is curry paste fried in coconut cream before the rest of the coconut milk is added?
quiz.a: Frying ('blooming') the paste in the fat-rich cream releases and intensifies its aromatic oils before diluting with more liquid

modules.pro_tip: Don't shake the coconut milk can; scoop the thick cream off the top first to fry the paste properly.

modules.title: Middle Eastern Technique: Spice Blends and Hummus
modules.description: Middle Eastern cooking relies on layered spice blends like za'atar and baharat, and on emulsified purees like hummus, made from blended chickpeas, tahini, lemon, and garlic. This lesson covers building a smooth, well-balanced hummus.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Middle Eastern Technique: Spice Blends and Hummus
Middle Eastern cooking relies on layered spice blends like za'atar and baharat, and on emulsified purees like hummus, made from blended chickpeas, tahini, lemon, and garlic.

modules.title: Middle Eastern Classic: Shakshuka
modules.description: Shakshuka is a North African and Middle Eastern dish of eggs poached directly in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce, demonstrating how to poach delicate eggs in a thick simmering sauce rather than water. This lesson covers building the sauce and timing the eggs.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Middle Eastern Classic: Shakshuka

Shakshuka is a North African and Middle Eastern dish of eggs poached directly in a spiced tomato and pepper sauce, demonstrating how to poach delicate eggs in a thick simmering sauce rather than water.
steps: Saute onion and pepper until softened, then add garlic and spices
Add tomatoes and simmer until thickened into a rich sauce, about 15-20 minutes
Make small wells in the sauce and crack eggs directly into them
Cover and cook gently until egg whites are set but yolks remain runny
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Middle Eastern Classic: Shakshuka" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does the sauce need to thicken before the eggs are added?
quiz.a: A thin sauce won't support poaching eggs properly and will make the dish watery instead of rich

modules.pro_tip: Cover the pan while the eggs poach so the whites cook through evenly on top without flipping.

modules.title: Korean Technique: Fermentation and Kimchi Basics
modules.description: Kimchi is a fermented Korean side dish, most commonly made from napa cabbage salted, seasoned with gochugaru (chili flakes), garlic, ginger, and fish sauce, then left to ferment, developing tangy, complex flavor over days. This lesson introduces basic fermentation safety and process.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Korean Technique: Fermentation and Kimchi Basics

Kimchi is a fermented Korean side dish, most commonly made from napa cabbage salted, seasoned with gochugaru (chili flakes), garlic, ginger, and fish sauce, then left to ferment, developing tangy, complex flavor over days.
steps: Salt the cabbage generously and let it sit until wilted and flexible, rinsing off excess salt after
Mix a paste of gochugaru, garlic, ginger, and fish sauce
Massage the paste thoroughly into the cabbage, coating every leaf
Pack tightly into a jar, pressing out air, and let ferment at room temperature for 1-5 days before refrigerating
materials_needed: Garlic, ginger, fish sauce or fermented shrimp
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Korean Technique: Fermentation and Kimchi Basics" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is the cabbage salted and wilted before seasoning rather than used raw and crisp?
quiz.a: Salting draws out excess water and softens the cabbage so it can absorb the seasoning paste and ferment properly

modules.pro_tip: Press the packed kimchi down so liquid rises above the solids, which limits oxygen exposure and unwanted mold growth.

modules.title: Mediterranean Technique: Grilling Fish Whole
modules.description: Mediterranean cooking often grills whole fish simply, with olive oil, lemon, and herbs, letting the fish's own flavor shine while the skin crisps and protects the delicate flesh. This lesson covers preparing and grilling a whole fish safely.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Mediterranean Technique: Grilling Fish Whole
Mediterranean cooking often grills whole fish simply, with olive oil, lemon, and herbs, letting the fish's own flavor shine while the skin crisps and protects the delicate flesh.
steps: Pat the fish very dry and score the skin a few times on each side
Rub generously with olive oil, salt, and stuff the cavity with lemon and herbs
Oil the grill grates well and place the fish over medium-high direct heat
Grill undisturbed until the skin releases easily, then flip once and finish on the other side
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Mediterranean Technique: Grilling Fish Whole" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is oiling both the fish and the grill grates important?

modules.pro_tip: Wait until the fish releases naturally from the grate before flipping; forcing it too early tears the skin.

modules.title: Mediterranean Classic: Paella
modules.description: Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked in a wide, shallow pan, prized for the crispy caramelized rice layer at the bottom called socarrat, traditionally made with saffron, seafood or rabbit and chicken, and short-grain rice. This lesson covers building the dish and achieving socarrat.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Mediterranean Classic: Paella

Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked in a wide, shallow pan, prized for the crispy caramelized rice layer at the bottom called socarrat, traditionally made with saffron, seafood or rabbit and chicken, and short-grain rice.
steps: Sear protein and saute aromatics directly in the wide paella pan
Add rice and stir briefly to coat it in the flavorful fat
Add hot saffron-infused broth in the correct ratio and do not stir again
Simmer undisturbed, then increase heat briefly at the end to form the crispy socarrat crust on the bottom
materials_needed: Protein of choice (chicken, seafood, or rabbit)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Mediterranean Classic: Paella" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is 'socarrat' in paella, and how is it achieved?
quiz.a: The crispy, caramelized layer of rice at the bottom of the pan, formed by briefly increasing heat near the end and not stirring

modules.pro_tip: Resist the urge to stir paella once the broth is added; stirring releases starch and prevents socarrat from forming.

modules.title: Baking Advanced: Laminated Dough (Croissants)
modules.description: Laminated dough is built by folding butter into dough repeatedly to create hundreds of thin alternating layers, which puff dramatically in the oven as steam separates them, producing croissants and puff pastry. This lesson introduces the lamination and folding process.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Baking Advanced: Laminated Dough (Croissants)

Laminated dough is built by folding butter into dough repeatedly to create hundreds of thin alternating layers, which puff dramatically in the oven as steam separates them, producing croissants and puff pastry.
steps: Encase a flat block of cold butter inside the rolled-out dough
Roll the dough out into a long rectangle, keeping it cold and even
Fold it into thirds (a 'letter fold') and chill for at least 30 minutes
Repeat rolling and folding several times, chilling between each, to build up thin layers
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Baking Advanced: Laminated Dough (Croissants)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why must the dough be chilled between each fold in lamination?
quiz.a: Chilling keeps the butter firm and distinct from the dough, preventing it from melting into the dough and losing its layered structure

modules.pro_tip: Work in a cool kitchen and chill often; if butter starts melting into the dough, the lamination is ruined.

modules.title: Advanced Technique: Butchering and Breaking Down a Chicken
modules.description: Breaking down a whole chicken into parts (breasts, thighs, wings, drumsticks) is a fundamental butchery skill that saves money and improves cooking control since each part can be cooked to its own ideal method. This lesson covers safe joint-finding technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Advanced Technique: Butchering and Breaking Down a Chicken

Breaking down a whole chicken into parts (breasts, thighs, wings, drumsticks) is a fundamental butchery skill that saves money and improves cooking control since each part can be cooked to its own ideal method.
steps: Remove the legs by cutting through the skin between leg and body, then popping the joint and cutting through
Separate the thigh from the drumstick by cutting through the connecting joint
Remove each wing by cutting through its shoulder joint close to the body
Cut along both sides of the breastbone to release the two breast halves
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Advanced Technique: Butchering and Breaking Down a Chicken" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is it better to cut through a joint rather than through bone when butchering poultry?
quiz.a: Joints are soft cartilage and separate easily with a knife, while cutting through bone requires much more force and can shatter it

modules.pro_tip: Feel for the joint with your fingers first and let the knife find that natural gap rather than forcing through bone.

modules.title: Advanced Technique: Filleting a Round Fish
modules.description: Filleting removes the two boneless sides of a fish from its central skeleton, a precise knife skill that maximizes usable flesh and minimizes waste, applicable to fish like salmon or trout. This lesson covers the standard filleting cut sequence.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Advanced Technique: Filleting a Round Fish
Filleting removes the two boneless sides of a fish from its central skeleton, a precise knife skill that maximizes usable flesh and minimizes waste, applicable to fish like salmon or trout.
steps: Cut behind the gills down to the backbone without cutting all the way through
Turn the knife flat and run it along the backbone from head to tail in one smooth motion
Lift the fillet away as you cut, keeping the blade angled toward the bones to preserve flesh
Repeat on the other side, then trim away any remaining pin bones with tweezers
materials_needed: Whole round fish, scaled and gutted
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Advanced Technique: Filleting a Round Fish" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does the fillet knife stay angled toward the fish's bones during the cut?
quiz.a: Angling toward the bones preserves as much flesh as possible on the fillet, minimizing waste

modules.pro_tip: Run a finger along the fillet after cutting to feel for remaining pin bones, then pull them out with tweezers or pliers.

modules.title: Advanced Baking: Tempering Chocolate
modules.description: Tempering chocolate carefully heats and cools it through specific temperatures to form stable cocoa butter crystals, giving finished chocolate a glossy shine and firm snap instead of a dull, soft, or streaky finish. This lesson covers the classic seed method.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Advanced Baking: Tempering Chocolate

Tempering chocolate carefully heats and cools it through specific temperatures to form stable cocoa butter crystals, giving finished chocolate a glossy shine and firm snap instead of a dull, soft, or streaky finish.
steps: Melt two-thirds of the chocolate gently, avoiding any water contact, to about 45-50C
Add the remaining solid chocolate (the 'seed') and stir until it cools to the working temperature, around 31-32C for dark chocolate
Test by dipping a spoon; properly tempered chocolate sets glossy and firm within a few minutes at room temperature
Keep the tempered chocolate within its working range while using it, gently rewarming if it cools too much
materials_needed: Marble slab or bowl for seeding
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Advanced Baking: Tempering Chocolate" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What causes chocolate that isn't tempered properly to look dull or streaky (bloom) once set?
quiz.a: Unstable cocoa butter crystals form, rather than the stable crystal structure created by careful temperature control

modules.pro_tip: Never let a single drop of water touch melting chocolate; even a tiny amount can cause it to seize and turn grainy.

modules.title: Advanced Technique: Curing and Preserving Food
modules.description: Curing uses salt, sugar, and sometimes nitrates to draw out moisture and inhibit bacterial growth, preserving foods like bacon, gravlax, and cured egg yolks while concentrating flavor. This lesson introduces basic dry-curing principles and food safety.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Advanced Technique: Curing and Preserving Food
Curing uses salt, sugar, and sometimes nitrates to draw out moisture and inhibit bacterial growth, preserving foods like bacon, gravlax, and cured egg yolks while concentrating flavor.
steps: Mix a curing blend of salt, sugar, and any flavorings like dill or pepper
Coat the protein evenly and completely in the cure mixture
Wrap tightly and refrigerate for the appropriate time, from a couple of days for gravlax to a week for bacon
Rinse off the cure thoroughly and pat dry before slicing or further cooking
materials_needed: Protein to cure (salmon for gravlax, pork belly for bacon)
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Advanced Technique: Curing and Preserving Food" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

skills.title: Call Emergency Services
skills.description: In an emergency, call your country's emergency number (999 UK, 911 USA, 112 Europe). Say your name, location, and what happened. Stay on the line.

skills.title: Treat a Small Cut
skills.description: Wash hands first. Run cut under clean water. Pat dry. Apply plaster. Tell an adult.

skills.title: Stranger Safety
skills.description: Never go with someone you don't know. Your safe adults are your parents, teachers, and trusted family. If you feel unsafe, go to a crowded place and ask for help.

quiz.question: What is the first thing to do in an emergency?
How do you treat a small cut?
options: Wash with water, dry, and apply a plaster

skills.title: The Recovery Position
skills.description: For an unconscious, breathing person: tilt head back gently, bend closest knee, roll them toward you onto their side, mouth facing down to prevent choking.
skills.why: Prevents choking on vomit in unconscious patients.

skills.title: Treat a Minor Burn
skills.description: Cool with running cold water for at least 10 minutes. Do NOT use ice, butter, or toothpaste. Cover loosely with clean wrap. Seek medical advice for anything larger than a 50p coin.
skills.why: Incorrect burn treatment causes more damage.

skills.title: Respond to Choking
skills.description: If someone is choking and cannot cough, give 5 back blows between shoulder blades. Then 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre). Repeat and call emergency services.
skills.why: Choking can be fatal without immediate action.

quiz.question: How long should you cool a burn with cold water?
What should you NEVER put on a burn?

skills.title: CPR Basics
skills.description: Check for danger, response, airway, breathing. If not breathing normally: 30 chest compressions (push hard and fast, 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 per minute), 2 rescue breaths. Continue until help arrives.
skills.why: CPR can double or triple survival chances after cardiac arrest.

skills.title: Recognise Anaphylaxis
skills.description: Signs: severe rash, swollen throat, difficulty breathing, dizziness. ACTION: Call 999 immediately. If prescribed, help use epinephrine auto-injector (EpiPen). Lay person flat, legs raised. Stay until ambulance arrives.
skills.why: Anaphylaxis can be fatal within minutes without treatment.

quiz.question: In CPR, how deep should chest compressions be for an adult?
What is the correct compression rate per minute in CPR?

skills.title: What is First Aid?
skills.explanation: Understand the purpose and limits of first aid.
steps: First aid helps someone who is injured or ill until professional help arrives.
Learn D-R-A-B-C: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation.
Always call emergency services (999 / 112) for serious incidents.
Stay calm so you can help others.
Never put yourself in danger.
skills.tip: D-R-A-B-C is a quick checklist to assess any situation.

quiz.question: What does the 'D' in D-R-A-B-C stand for?
When should you call 999?
options: For any serious illness or injury
Only if you know the person

skills.title: Treating Cuts and Grazes
steps: Wash your hands or use gloves if available.
Rinse the wound under clean running water.
Pat dry gently with a clean cloth.
Apply an antiseptic wipe if available.
Cover with a sterile plaster or bandage.
skills.tip: Do not pick at a scab — it protects the healing skin underneath.

quiz.question: First step when treating a cut?
What should you use to rinse a wound?

skills.title: Burns and Scalds
skills.explanation: Cool a burn and prevent infection.
steps: Cool the burn under cool (not cold/icy) running water for 10–20 minutes.
Do not use butter, oil, or toothpaste.
Remove jewellery near the burn if safe to do so.
Cover loosely with cling film or a clean plastic bag.
Seek medical help for burns larger than a 50p coin.
skills.tip: Never burst blisters — this increases infection risk.

quiz.question: How long should you cool a burn?
What should you NEVER put on a burn?

skills.title: Recovery Position
skills.explanation: Place an unconscious breathing person safely.
steps: Kneel beside the person.
Place the nearest arm at a right angle.
Bring the far hand to rest on the cheek.
Pull up the far knee and roll them towards you.
Tilt the head back to keep the airway open and call 999.
skills.tip: The recovery position prevents an unconscious person from choking on vomit.

quiz.question: Why use the recovery position?
options: To keep the airway open and prevent choking

quiz.question: What should you do after placing someone in recovery position?

skills.title: CPR Basics
skills.explanation: Understand chest compressions and rescue breaths.
steps: Check for danger and response.
Call 999 immediately.
Push down hard and fast on the centre of the chest — 30 compressions.
Give 2 rescue breaths (tilt head, lift chin, seal lips, blow).
Continue 30:2 until help arrives or the person recovers.
skills.tip: Push hard enough — at least 5–6 cm depth on an adult.

quiz.question: CPR compression to breath ratio is?
Where do you place hands for chest compressions?

modules.title: Calling for Emergency Help
modules.description: Knowing when and how to call emergency services is often the single most important first aid action. This lesson covers what information to give a dispatcher and how to stay calm and clear under pressure.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Calling for Emergency Help
Knowing when and how to call emergency services is often the single most important first aid action.
steps: Call your local emergency number (911, 999, 112, or similar depending on country)

modules.title: Hand Hygiene and Infection Prevention
modules.description: Proper handwashing and glove use prevent the spread of infection between the first aider and the injured person during any treatment. This lesson covers correct handwashing technique and when gloves are necessary.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Hand Hygiene and Infection Prevention
Proper handwashing and glove use prevent the spread of infection between the first aider and the injured person during any treatment.
steps: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before and after giving care

Put on disposable gloves before touching any wound, blood, or bodily fluid
Dispose of used gloves properly and wash hands again afterward
materials_needed: Soap and water or hand sanitizer
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Hand Hygiene and Infection Prevention" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap and water to be effective?
quiz.a: At least 20 seconds, covering all surfaces including between fingers and under nails

modules.pro_tip: Always assume any blood or bodily fluid could carry infection, and use gloves as a routine precaution.

modules.title: Recognizing an Emergency vs. a Minor Injury

learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Recognizing an Emergency vs. a Minor Injury

modules.title: Managing Nosebleeds
modules.description: Nosebleeds are common and usually not serious, but correct technique stops bleeding faster and reduces complications. This lesson covers the proper head position and pressure technique, correcting the common myth of tilting the head back.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Managing Nosebleeds
Nosebleeds are common and usually not serious, but correct technique stops bleeding faster and reduces complications.
steps: Sit the person up and lean them slightly forward, not backward
Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for a full 10 minutes without releasing
Have the person breathe through their mouth during this time
Apply a cold compress to the bridge of the nose to help slow bleeding
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Managing Nosebleeds" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why should the head be tilted forward, not backward, during a nosebleed?
quiz.a: Tilting back lets blood run down the throat, which can cause choking or vomiting instead of stopping the bleed

modules.pro_tip: Avoid checking on the nosebleed by releasing pressure early; a full 10 minutes uninterrupted works best.

modules.title: Applying a Sterile Dressing and Bandage
modules.description: Correctly applying a dressing controls bleeding and protects a wound from further contamination. This lesson covers dressing selection, application, and securing a bandage without cutting off circulation.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Applying a Sterile Dressing and Bandage
Correctly applying a dressing controls bleeding and protects a wound from further contamination.
steps: Cover the wound completely with a sterile dressing larger than the wound itself
Hold the dressing in place and wrap a roller bandage around it snugly, not too tight
Secure the end of the bandage with tape or a clip
Check fingers or toes below the bandage for color and warmth to ensure circulation isn't restricted
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Applying a Sterile Dressing and Bandage" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a bandage has been applied too tightly?
quiz.a: The area beyond it, like fingers or toes, becomes pale, blue, cold, numb, or swollen from restricted circulation

modules.pro_tip: Check circulation below any bandage a few minutes after applying it and periodically afterward.

modules.title: Controlling Severe Bleeding
modules.description: Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so applying firm direct pressure immediately is critical. This lesson covers direct pressure, wound packing, and when to escalate to a tourniquet.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Controlling Severe Bleeding
Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so applying firm direct pressure immediately is critical.
steps: Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth or gauze
Do not remove the cloth if it soaks through; add more layers on top and keep pressing
Elevate the injured area above heart level if possible and there's no suspected fracture
If bleeding is severe and uncontrolled by pressure, apply a tourniquet above the wound as a last resort
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Controlling Severe Bleeding" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What should you do if a bleeding wound soaks through your first dressing?
quiz.a: Leave the original dressing in place and add more layers on top rather than removing and re-checking it, which disturbs clotting

modules.pro_tip: Note the time a tourniquet is applied, since medical responders need this information.
modules.lesson_text:
Controlling Severe Bleeding is a skill worth learning properly rather than casually. Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so applying firm direct pressure immediately is critical. This lesson covers direct pressure, wound packing, and when to escalate to a tourniquet. This lesson walks through the skill from first principles: what it is, why it matters, what you need before you begin, how to work through it step by step, the mistakes that most commonly trip up beginners, and how to practise it until it becomes reliable under real conditions rather than something you can only do on a good day.

Before touching the steps, it helps to understand why this skill earns a place in the curriculum. Skills like this one compound: each hour of correct, focused practice makes the next hour more productive, and the habits you build here -- preparing properly, working in the right order, checking your results -- transfer directly to every other skill in this pathway. Learners who rush past the fundamentals usually have to come back and relearn them later, at greater cost. Taking the time to get the basic pattern right the first time is the single most efficient thing you can do.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: Controlling Severe Bleeding; Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes, so applying firm direct pressure immediately is critical. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: Clean cloth or gauze, Gloves, Tourniquet (commercial or improvised). Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

Now work through the core sequence. Take each step slowly the first several times; speed comes later, and comes faster if you don't chase it early. Step 1: Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth or gauze. Once this feels comfortable, try to notice what changed compared with your first attempt; that awareness is itself a skill and accelerates everything that follows. Step 2: Do not remove the cloth if it soaks through; add more layers on top and keep pressing. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly. Step 3: Elevate the injured area above heart level if possible and there's no suspected fracture. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence.

modules.title: Treating Sprains and Strains (RICE Method)
modules.description: Sprains (ligament injuries) and strains (muscle or tendon injuries) are common soft-tissue injuries that respond well to prompt, correct first aid. This lesson introduces the RICE method: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Treating Sprains and Strains (RICE Method)
Sprains (ligament injuries) and strains (muscle or tendon injuries) are common soft-tissue injuries that respond well to prompt, correct first aid.
steps: Rest the injured area and avoid putting weight or strain on it
Ice the area for 15-20 minutes at a time, with a cloth barrier to protect skin
Compress gently with an elastic bandage, wrapped snugly but not tight enough to cut off circulation
Elevate the injured limb above heart level when possible to reduce swelling
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Treating Sprains and Strains (RICE Method)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What does each letter in RICE stand for when treating a sprain?
quiz.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation

modules.pro_tip: Never apply ice directly to bare skin; always use a cloth or towel barrier to prevent ice burn.

modules.title: Recognizing and Splinting a Suspected Fracture
modules.description: A suspected broken bone should be immobilized in the position found to prevent further injury while awaiting medical care. This lesson covers signs of a fracture and basic splinting technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Recognizing and Splinting a Suspected Fracture
A suspected broken bone should be immobilized in the position found to prevent further injury while awaiting medical care.
steps: Look for signs of fracture: deformity, severe pain, swelling, or inability to move the limb
Support the limb above and below the injury without trying to straighten it
Pad a rigid splint and place it alongside the limb, immobilizing the joints above and below the break
Secure the splint with bandages, checking circulation regularly, and seek medical care immediately
materials_needed: Rigid material for a splint (board, rolled magazine)
Bandage or tape to secure the splint
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Recognizing and Splinting a Suspected Fracture" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why should you never try to straighten a suspected broken bone?
quiz.a: Moving or realigning it can cause further damage to bones, nerves, blood vessels, or surrounding tissue

modules.pro_tip: Splint the limb in the position it was found rather than attempting to reposition it first.

modules.title: Recognizing Signs of Shock
modules.description: Shock is a life-threatening condition where the body's organs aren't getting enough blood flow, often following severe injury or blood loss, and requires prompt recognition and care. This lesson covers symptoms and initial response.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Recognizing Signs of Shock
Shock is a life-threatening condition where the body's organs aren't getting enough blood flow, often following severe injury or blood loss, and requires prompt recognition and care.
steps: Watch for signs of shock: pale or cool skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid breathing, and confusion
Lay the person down and, if no spinal or leg injury is suspected, elevate their legs slightly
Keep the person warm with a blanket and calm and reassured
Call emergency services immediately, as shock can worsen quickly without treatment
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Recognizing Signs of Shock" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What are three key warning signs of shock?
quiz.a: Any three of: pale/cool/clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing, confusion, or weakness

modules.pro_tip: Do not give a person in shock food or water, as they may need surgery and could also vomit or choke.

modules.title: Treating Insect Stings and Bites
modules.description: Most insect stings and bites are minor, but some can trigger dangerous allergic reactions, so it's important to know both routine care and warning signs. This lesson covers safe stinger removal and monitoring for reaction.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Treating Insect Stings and Bites
Most insect stings and bites are minor, but some can trigger dangerous allergic reactions, so it's important to know both routine care and warning signs.
steps: If a stinger is visible, scrape it out sideways with a card rather than squeezing with tweezers
Wash the area with soap and water
Apply a cold compress to reduce swelling and pain
Watch closely for signs of a serious allergic reaction over the following 30-60 minutes
materials_needed: Card or flat object for scraping
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Treating Insect Stings and Bites" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is scraping a stinger out preferred over pulling it with tweezers?
quiz.a: Squeezing the stinger can push more venom into the skin, while scraping removes it without added pressure

modules.pro_tip: Keep a close eye on anyone stung for signs of a severe allergic reaction, even if they've never reacted before.

modules.title: Basic CPR Technique for Adults
modules.description: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) keeps oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and vital organs when the heart has stopped, dramatically improving survival chances if started immediately. This lesson covers the compression technique and rate for adults.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Basic CPR Technique for Adults
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) keeps oxygenated blood circulating to the brain and vital organs when the heart has stopped, dramatically improving survival chances if started immediately.
steps: Check for responsiveness and normal breathing; call emergency services or have someone else call
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, fingers interlaced
Push hard and fast, at least 5cm (2 inches) deep, at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute
Allow the chest to fully recoil between compressions, minimizing interruptions until help arrives or the person recovers

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of chest compressions per minute in adult CPR?
