Basic Breakfalls (Ukemi) looks simple when someone experienced does it -- and that is exactly why it deserves careful study. Breakfalls, called ukemi, teach practitioners how to fall safely and absorb impact without injury, and this is one of the first skills taught in any grappling art before takedowns are introduced. Learning to slap the mat and tuck the chin protects the head, neck, and joints when being taken down. This lesson covers backward, sideways, and forward rolling breakfalls. In this lesson you will break the skill into learnable parts, practise each part slowly and deliberately, and then reassemble them into a smooth whole, which is how experienced practitioners in every field actually build their fluency.

A word on why this topic is taught the way it is. Research on skill acquisition consistently shows that people learn physical and procedural skills best in three phases: first understanding what correct execution looks like, then practising slowly with full attention to form, and finally adding speed, pressure, or complexity only after the basic pattern is stable. This lesson is organised around exactly that progression, so resist the temptation to skip ahead -- the order is doing real work.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: Basic Breakfalls (Ukemi); Breakfalls, called ukemi, teach practitioners how to fall safely and absorb impact without injury, and this is one of the first skills taught in any grappling art before takedowns are introduced. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: mats. Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

Here is the step-by-step method. As you work through it, narrate each step to yourself in your own words -- explaining as you go is one of the most reliable ways to move a procedure from short-term memory into lasting skill. Step 1: Practice the backward breakfall: tuck chin, round the back, and slap the mat with both arms as you land. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence. Step 2: Practice the side breakfall, landing on one arm and the side of the body flat against the mat. There is no prize for hurrying this step -- accuracy first, then rhythm, then speed, in that order. Step 3: Practice a forward rolling breakfall, rolling diagonally across one shoulder rather than landing flat. Once this feels comfortable, try to notice what changed compared with your first attempt; that awareness is itself a skill and accelerates everything that follows. Step 4: Drill each breakfall slowly under supervision before increasing speed. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly.

Frustration after early failure leads people to conclude they lack talent, when in fact almost every stumble at this stage is simply a step being taken too fast or out of order. Steady, modest, correct practice beats occasional heroic effort by a wide margin.

modules.title: Solo Movement Drills: The Hip Escape (Shrimping)
modules.description: The hip escape, commonly called shrimping, is a foundational movement used to create space between you and an opponent while on the ground, and it underlies nearly every escape and guard retention technique in BJJ. Practicing it as a solo drill builds the hip mobility and body mechanics needed before applying it against resistance. This lesson introduces the movement pattern.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Solo Movement Drills: The Hip Escape (Shrimping)

The hip escape, commonly called shrimping, is a foundational movement used to create space between you and an opponent while on the ground, and it underlies nearly every escape and guard retention technique in BJJ.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the mat
Post on one hand and foot, and push your hips away from that side, creating a shrimp-like motion
Bring the far knee toward your elbow to frame space, then repeat on the other side
Practice moving the length of the mat using continuous shrimping
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Solo Movement Drills: The Hip Escape (Shrimping)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of the hip escape (shrimping) movement in BJJ?
quiz.a: To create space between yourself and an opponent so you can escape a bad position or recover guard

modules.pro_tip: Drill shrimping as a warm-up every class; it's a movement you'll use constantly once you begin rolling.

modules.title: Bridging (Upa) Movement
modules.description: Bridging, called upa, is a powerful hip-driving movement used to unseat an opponent's weight or base, most famously as the foundation of the mount escape. It generates power from the hips and legs rather than the arms, which is a core principle of leverage-based grappling. This lesson introduces the bridging motion as a solo and partnered drill.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Bridging (Upa) Movement
Bridging, called upa, is a powerful hip-driving movement used to unseat an opponent's weight or base, most famously as the foundation of the mount escape.
steps: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet planted close to your hips
Drive through your feet and arch your hips explosively upward off the mat
Practice bridging to one side to add a rotational component
With a partner lightly on top, practice bridging them off-balance under controlled supervision
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Bridging (Upa) Movement" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What part of the body generates the power in a bridge (upa) movement?
quiz.a: The hips and legs, driving upward and through the feet, not the arms

modules.pro_tip: Keep your feet close to your hips before bridging; feet placed too far away weakens the movement's power.

modules.title: The Technical Stand-Up
modules.description: The technical stand-up is the safest way to return to your feet from the ground while keeping a hand and eyes on a training partner, which matters both for sport grappling and self-defense. It avoids turning your back or momentarily losing sight of the other person, unlike simply scrambling upright. This lesson covers the step-by-step technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Technical Stand-Up
The technical stand-up is the safest way to return to your feet from the ground while keeping a hand and eyes on a training partner, which matters both for sport grappling and self-defense.
steps: From a seated position, post one hand behind you and place the same-side foot flat on the ground
Push through that hand and foot to raise your hips, sliding the other leg back
Come to a standing base with hands up, keeping eyes on your partner throughout
Practice from both sides until the movement feels natural
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Technical Stand-Up" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does the technical stand-up avoid turning your back to the other person?
quiz.a: Turning away removes your ability to see and react to what they're doing, which is a safety risk in both sport and self-defense contexts

modules.pro_tip: Practice the technical stand-up until it's automatic -- it's one of the most frequently used movements in live training.

modules.title: Closed Guard Basics
modules.description: The closed guard is a fundamental position where the bottom practitioner wraps their legs around the opponent's waist and locks their ankles, controlling distance and preventing the opponent from standing or passing easily. It's typically one of the first defensive and offensive positions taught to beginners. This lesson covers entering and understanding the closed guard.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Closed Guard Basics

The closed guard is a fundamental position where the bottom practitioner wraps their legs around the opponent's waist and locks their ankles, controlling distance and preventing the opponent from standing or passing easily.
steps: From the ground, wrap both legs around your partner's waist and cross your ankles behind their back
Keep your hips close to theirs to reduce space for them to posture or escape
Use grips on the sleeves, collar, or wrists to control their posture
Practice maintaining the position calmly while your partner attempts to posture up
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Closed Guard Basics" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of crossing your ankles behind an opponent's back in closed guard?
quiz.a: It locks your legs together to control distance and prevent the opponent from standing up or creating space to pass

modules.pro_tip: A strong closed guard controls the opponent's posture first; without posture control, sweeps and submissions become much harder.

modules.title: Guard Retention Fundamentals
modules.description: Guard retention is the skill of preventing an opponent from passing your guard and advancing to a dominant position, relying on constant hip movement, framing with the arms, and rebuilding distance. It's considered one of the most important defensive skills in modern BJJ. This lesson introduces the core concepts of retaining guard against a passing opponent.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Guard Retention Fundamentals
Guard retention is the skill of preventing an opponent from passing your guard and advancing to a dominant position, relying on constant hip movement, framing with the arms, and rebuilding distance.
steps: Use frames (forearms braced against the opponent's hips or shoulders) to maintain distance

modules.title: Escaping Mount: The Elbow-Knee (Shrimp) Escape
modules.description: Being mounted is one of the most dominant positions an opponent can achieve, and the elbow-knee escape uses hip movement and frames to recover guard rather than trying to muscle the opponent off. This lesson covers the step-by-step shrimp escape from mount.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Escaping Mount: The Elbow-Knee (Shrimp) Escape

steps: Frame an arm across the opponent's hip or thigh to prevent them from sliding forward
Bridge slightly to create space, then shrimp your hips out to one side

modules.title: Escaping Side Control: Recovering Guard
modules.description: Once framing and shrimping have created enough space in side control, the next step is reinserting a leg or knee to rebuild guard, restoring a neutral or advantageous position. This lesson covers finishing the escape and re-establishing guard.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Escaping Side Control: Recovering Guard
Once framing and shrimping have created enough space in side control, the next step is reinserting a leg or knee to rebuild guard, restoring a neutral or advantageous position.
steps: Continue shrimping until there is enough space to bring a knee between you and the opponent

quiz.q: What is the escape's goal once space has been created in side control?

modules.title: Passing the Closed Guard: The Standing Pass
modules.description: Standing up inside an opponent's closed guard is one of the most common ways to begin a guard pass, using the extra distance and gravity to help break the guard open. This lesson covers standing safely and opening the guard from a standing base.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Passing the Closed Guard: The Standing Pass
Standing up inside an opponent's closed guard is one of the most common ways to begin a guard pass, using the extra distance and gravity to help break the guard open.
steps: Maintain good posture, then place one foot back and stand up while controlling the opponent's hips or sleeves
Once standing, use your hands to push the opponent's knees down and apart to open the guard
Step around or over a leg to begin passing to a dominant position such as side control
Stay balanced and controlled throughout, avoiding falling into the opponent's guard again
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Passing the Closed Guard: The Standing Pass" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does standing up help when opening a closed guard?
quiz.a: It uses gravity and distance to make it harder for the opponent to maintain their grip and leg control, making the guard easier to open

modules.pro_tip: Keep your base wide and stable when standing in someone's guard; a narrow stance is easy to off-balance.

modules.description: The knee slide pass is a fundamental technique that uses hip pressure and a sliding knee motion to pass from inside an opened guard to side control while staying low and heavy. This lesson covers the mechanics of this classic passing technique.

modules.title: Passing Open Guard: The Torreando (Bullfighter) Pass
modules.description: The torreando or bullfighter pass controls both of the opponent's pant legs or shins and redirects their legs to one side while stepping around to the other, similar to a bullfighter avoiding a charging bull. This lesson covers this widely used open guard passing technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Passing Open Guard: The Torreando (Bullfighter) Pass

The torreando or bullfighter pass controls both of the opponent's pant legs or shins and redirects their legs to one side while stepping around to the other, similar to a bullfighter avoiding a charging bull.
steps: Grip both of the opponent's pant legs or shins firmly
Push their legs to one side while stepping quickly around to the opposite side
Keep the grips controlled until your hips clear their legs completely
Settle into side control or knee-on-belly once past their legs
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Passing Open Guard: The Torreando (Bullfighter) Pass" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What does the torreando pass redirect in order to move around the opponent's legs?
quiz.a: The opponent's legs, pushing them to one side while stepping to the other, similar to a bullfighter's redirection

modules.pro_tip: Move quickly and decisively during a torreando pass -- hesitating in the middle gives the opponent time to re-guard.

modules.title: The Scissor Sweep
modules.description: The scissor sweep is a classic sweep from closed guard that uses a scissoring leg motion combined with an off-balancing grip to take the opponent from top to bottom. It's often one of the first sweeps taught because it clearly teaches the principle of off-balancing an opponent using leverage rather than strength. This lesson covers the full mechanics.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Scissor Sweep
The scissor sweep is a classic sweep from closed guard that uses a scissoring leg motion combined with an off-balancing grip to take the opponent from top to bottom.
steps: From closed guard, open your guard and angle your body to one side
Place one shin across the opponent's stomach and the other leg low behind their same-side knee
Grip their same-side sleeve and opposite collar or shoulder to control their upper body
Scissor your legs in opposite directions while pulling with your grips to sweep them onto their back
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Scissor Sweep" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Which two body parts does the sweep 'scissor' in opposite directions to off-balance the opponent?
quiz.a: The legs -- one shin across the stomach pushing, the other behind the knee sweeping, moving in opposite directions

modules.pro_tip: Time the grip pull and the leg scissor to happen together; if they're out of sync the sweep loses much of its power.

modules.title: The Hip Bump Sweep
modules.description: The hip bump sweep is executed from closed guard by sitting up and driving the hips into the opponent while they're posted on one arm, taking advantage of a moment when their base is compromised. This lesson covers recognizing the opportunity and executing the sweep.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Hip Bump Sweep
The hip bump sweep is executed from closed guard by sitting up and driving the hips into the opponent while they're posted on one arm, taking advantage of a moment when their base is compromised.
steps: From closed guard, notice when the opponent posts one hand on the mat for balance
Sit up toward the posted-hand side while opening your guard
Drive your hip into their same-side hip, pushing their base out from under them
Follow them to the mount position as they fall backward
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Hip Bump Sweep" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What condition makes an opponent vulnerable to the hip bump sweep?
quiz.a: When they post one hand on the mat, temporarily narrowing their base on that side

modules.pro_tip: Watch for a partner's posted hand as your cue -- the hip bump sweep depends on that specific base weakness.

modules.title: The Flower Sweep (Pendulum Sweep)
modules.description: The flower sweep, also called the pendulum sweep, isolates one of the opponent's arms and uses a pendulum-like leg swing to off-balance them over that trapped arm. It's a technical sweep that teaches the principle of removing an opponent's base point before applying leverage. This lesson covers the setup and execution.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Flower Sweep (Pendulum Sweep)
The flower sweep, also called the pendulum sweep, isolates one of the opponent's arms and uses a pendulum-like leg swing to off-balance them over that trapped arm.
steps: From closed guard, control one of the opponent's wrists and trap it against your chest or hip
Open your guard and swing one leg up and over like a pendulum
Use the swinging leg's momentum combined with the trapped arm to roll the opponent over that shoulder
Follow through to a mount or side control position
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Flower Sweep (Pendulum Sweep)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is trapping one of the opponent's arms essential before the flower sweep?
quiz.a: It removes one of their potential posts or bases, so when the sweep is applied they have no way to catch themselves on that side

modules.pro_tip: Control the wrist tightly throughout the sweep; if the opponent frees their trapped arm they can often post and stop the sweep.

The flower sweep, also called the pendulum sweep, isolates one of the opponent's arms and uses a pendulum-like leg swing to off-balance them over that trapped arm. It's a technical sweep that teaches the principle of removing an opponent's base point before applying leverage. This lesson covers the setup and execution. In this lesson you will break the skill into learnable parts, practise each part slowly and deliberately, and then reassemble them into a smooth whole, which is how experienced practitioners in every field actually build their fluency.

A word on why this topic is taught the way it is. Research on skill acquisition consistently shows that people learn physical and procedural skills best in three phases: first understanding what correct execution looks like, then practising slowly with full attention to form, and finally adding speed, pressure, or complexity only after the basic pattern is stable. This lesson is organised around exactly that progression, so resist the temptation to skip ahead -- the order is doing real work.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: The Flower Sweep (Pendulum Sweep); The flower sweep, also called the pendulum sweep, isolates one of the opponent's arms and uses a pendulum-like leg swing to off-balance them over that trapped arm. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: gi (optional), training partner. Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

Here is the step-by-step method. As you work through it, narrate each step to yourself in your own words -- explaining as you go is one of the most reliable ways to move a procedure from short-term memory into lasting skill. Step 1: From closed guard, control one of the opponent's wrists and trap it against your chest or hip. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly. Step 2: Open your guard and swing one leg up and over like a pendulum. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing. Step 3: Use the swinging leg's momentum combined with the trapped arm to roll the opponent over that shoulder. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence. Step 4: Follow through to a mount or side control position. There is no prize for hurrying this step -- accuracy first, then rhythm, then speed, in that order.

Watch for the classic failure modes. Overconfidence after early success leads people to add speed or difficulty before the foundation is stable, and progress collapses. Frustration after early failure leads people to conclude they lack talent, when in fact almost every stumble at this stage is simply a step being taken too fast or out of order. And inconsistency -- practising intensely once and then not at all for weeks -- wastes most of the effort invested, because skills consolidate through repetition spaced over time. Steady, modest, correct practice beats occasional heroic effort by a wide margin.

A note on safety and good judgement: Control the wrist tightly throughout the sweep; if the opponent frees their trapped arm they can often post and stop the sweep. Build this into how you practise from the very first session, because safety habits are learned exactly the way every other habit is learned -- through repetition -- and it is far easier to build the careful version now than to retrofit it later.

Your practice assignment: Practice "The Flower Sweep (Pendulum Sweep)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed. After each session, spend one minute on deliberate review: what went well, what broke down, and what single thing you will focus on next time. This tiny habit -- professionals call it a debrief -- is the highest-leverage minute in the entire practice session, because it converts experience into insight while the details are still fresh.

Test yourself: Why is trapping one of the opponent's arms essential before the flower sweep? If your answer matches 'It removes one of their potential posts or bases, so when the sweep is applied they have no way to catch themselves on that side' and, more importantly, you can explain why, you are ready to continue. If not, revisit the steps above -- the gap is almost always in one specific step, and finding it now is cheap compared with finding it later.

When you feel ready to advance, resist the urge to jump to something entirely new. The efficient path is to deepen this skill first: perform it more smoothly, from memory, under less forgiving conditions, or while explaining it aloud to someone else. Teaching, even informally, is the fastest known test of real understanding -- gaps that hide during solo practice become obvious the moment you try to explain a step. When you can teach this lesson convincingly, you have genuinely learned it.

Remember where this sits in the wider Jiu-Jitsu pathway: the lessons before it built the context this one relies on, and the lessons after it will assume the ability you are building now. If any prerequisite feels shaky, a quick review before the next session is cheap insurance.

To close: aim for progress, not perfection. The standard to hold yourself to is simple -- a little more correct, a little more confident, and a little more consistent than last session. Skills built that way do not evaporate under stress, because they were never memorised tricks in the first place; they were understood. modules.title: Butterfly Guard Basics and the Butterfly Sweep
modules.description: Butterfly guard uses hooks with the feet or shins inside the opponent's thighs while sitting up, giving strong lifting and off-balancing leverage, especially useful in no-gi grappling. This lesson introduces the butterfly guard position and its signature sweep.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Butterfly Guard Basics and the Butterfly Sweep
Butterfly guard uses hooks with the feet or shins inside the opponent's thighs while sitting up, giving strong lifting and off-balancing leverage, especially useful in no-gi grappling.
steps: Sit up facing the opponent with both feet hooked inside their thighs
Establish an underhook or grip control on one side of their upper body
Lift with the hook while off-balancing them toward the controlled side
Follow the opponent over as they fall, transitioning to a dominant top position
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Butterfly Guard Basics and the Butterfly Sweep" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What makes butterfly guard's hooks especially effective for generating lifting power?
quiz.a: The feet hooked inside the thighs let you use your legs to lift and off-balance the opponent, which is stronger than using arms alone

modules.pro_tip: Butterfly guard works well in both gi and no-gi grappling since it doesn't rely on cloth grips to function.

modules.title: Achieving and Maintaining the Mount
modules.description: The mount is a dominant position where the top practitioner sits astride the opponent's torso with knees on the mat, offering strong control and multiple attacking options. Maintaining mount against a bridging, shrimping opponent requires good base and hip mobility. This lesson covers entering and holding mount.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Achieving and Maintaining the Mount
The mount is a dominant position where the top practitioner sits astride the opponent's torso with knees on the mat, offering strong control and multiple attacking options.
steps: Sit astride the opponent's torso with your knees pinched close to their body
Keep your weight centered and hips low to resist being bridged off
Post your hands or hook your feet under their legs to add stability against escapes
Follow their hip movement with your own hips rather than staying rigid
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Achieving and Maintaining the Mount" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is a key base principle for maintaining mount against a bridging opponent?
quiz.a: Keeping the knees pinched in and hips low and mobile, moving with the opponent's hips rather than staying rigid

modules.pro_tip: A high, upright mount can be more easily bridged off; a low, controlled mount with good base is more stable.

modules.title: Achieving and Maintaining Side Control
modules.description: Side control is a dominant pinning position where the top practitioner is perpendicular to the opponent, controlling their hips and shoulders while pinning their chest to the mat. This lesson covers proper weight distribution and control points for a stable side control.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Achieving and Maintaining Side Control
Side control is a dominant pinning position where the top practitioner is perpendicular to the opponent, controlling their hips and shoulders while pinning their chest to the mat.
steps: Pin the opponent's chest with your own chest, staying perpendicular to their body
Control their far hip with one arm and their far shoulder or head with the other
Keep your weight distributed heavily but with knees ready to adjust as they move
Transition your hips and weight to counter their escape attempts as needed
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Achieving and Maintaining Side Control" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What two control points does a strong side control typically secure?
quiz.a: The opponent's far hip and far shoulder (or head), preventing them from turning into you

modules.pro_tip: Stay heavy and mobile at the same time in side control -- rigid pressure without adjustment is easier to escape.

modules.title: The Triangle Choke (Sankaku Jime)
modules.description: The triangle choke, called sankaku jime, uses the legs to form a triangle shape around the opponent's neck and one arm, using their own shoulder to help compress the opposite carotid artery. learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Triangle Choke (Sankaku Jime)

modules.title: The Kimura Lock
modules.description: The kimura is a shoulder lock that rotates the opponent's arm behind their back using a figure-four grip on the wrist and bicep, and it can be applied from several positions including guard and side control. It's named after judoka Masahiko Kimura, who famously used it to defeat Hélio Gracie. This lesson covers the grip and application.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Kimura Lock

The kimura is a shoulder lock that rotates the opponent's arm behind their back using a figure-four grip on the wrist and bicep, and it can be applied from several positions including guard and side control.
steps: Control the opponent's wrist with one hand and reach under their elbow with your other arm
Grip your own wrist to form a figure-four lock on their arm
Keep their elbow close to their body and rotate the wrist toward their back slowly
Apply pressure gradually and release the instant your partner taps
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Kimura Lock" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: After whom is the kimura lock named, and what is he known for regarding the technique?
quiz.a: Judoka Masahiko Kimura, who used the technique to defeat Hélio Gracie in a famous 1951 match

modules.pro_tip: Keep the opponent's elbow pinned close to their body throughout a kimura; if it drifts away the lock loses much of its leverage.

modules.title: The Americana (Keylock)
modules.description: The americana, or keylock, is a shoulder lock applied by pinning an opponent's arm in a bent, right-angle position and levering it upward toward their head, commonly taught from side control or mount. This lesson covers the grip and safe, gradual application.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Americana (Keylock)

The americana, or keylock, is a shoulder lock applied by pinning an opponent's arm in a bent, right-angle position and levering it upward toward their head, commonly taught from side control or mount.
steps: Control the opponent's wrist and pin their upper arm to the mat, bending the elbow to roughly a right angle
Reach your other hand under their elbow and grip your own wrist, forming a figure-four
Slide the arm along the mat in an S-shaped path toward their head
Apply pressure gradually and release immediately when your partner taps
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Americana (Keylock)" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: In what general shape is the opponent's arm positioned before an americana is applied?
quiz.a: Bent at roughly a right angle, arm out to the side, similar to a goalpost or 'stick 'em up' shape

modules.pro_tip: The americana relies on a slow, controlled S-shaped motion, not a jerking one -- rushing it increases injury risk for your partner.

modules.title: The Guillotine Choke
modules.description: The guillotine is a front headlock choke applied when an opponent's head is trapped under your arm, often after a failed takedown attempt or when they shoot in low, compressing the front of the neck or the sides depending on the grip variation. This lesson covers the standard grip and safe application.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Guillotine Choke

The guillotine is a front headlock choke applied when an opponent's head is trapped under your arm, often after a failed takedown attempt or when they shoot in low, compressing the front of the neck or the sides depending on the grip variation.
steps: Trap the opponent's head under one arm as they duck their head forward or shoot in
Clasp your hands together under their chin, or grip your own wrist for the arm-in variation
Pull upward and back with your arms while arching your hips forward and squeezing your knees together for guard control
Apply pressure gradually and release immediately when your partner taps
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Guillotine Choke" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: In what common scenario does a guillotine choke opportunity often present itself?
quiz.a: When an opponent lowers or ducks their head, such as during a failed takedown attempt, trapping it under the arm

modules.pro_tip: Control the opponent's posture with your legs while applying a guillotine from guard; without hip control they can often posture out or stack you.

modules.title: Combining a Standing Guard Break with a Pass
modules.description: Rather than treating opening the guard and passing as two separate steps, advancing practitioners learn to chain a standing guard break directly into a passing sequence, minimizing the time an opponent has to reset or attack. learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Combining a Standing Guard Break with a Pass

Rather than treating opening the guard and passing as two separate steps, advancing practitioners learn to chain a standing guard break directly into a passing sequence, minimizing the time an opponent has to reset or attack.
steps: Stand up inside the closed guard while maintaining a stable base and grip control
Break the guard open by pushing the knees down and to the side in one motion
Immediately step or slide into a passing technique, such as the knee slide or torreando, without pausing
Settle into a stable pinning position once the pass is complete
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Combining a Standing Guard Break with a Pass" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is minimizing the pause between opening the guard and beginning the pass considered good technique?
quiz.a: A pause gives the opponent time to reset their guard, attack a leg, or set up a submission before the pass is complete

modules.title: Half Guard Basics
modules.description: Half guard is a position where the bottom player controls one of the opponent's legs between both of their own, offering both defensive control and sweep or submission opportunities. It sits between full guard and being passed, and understanding it helps prevent a stalled half guard from becoming a lost position. This lesson introduces the position and basic control points.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Half Guard Basics
Half guard is a position where the bottom player controls one of the opponent's legs between both of their own, offering both defensive control and sweep or submission opportunities.
steps: Trap one of the opponent's legs tightly between both of your own legs
Establish an underhook on the near side to prevent them from flattening you out
Keep your head and shoulders active, avoiding lying flat on your back
Use frames and hip movement to prevent the top player from passing further
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Half Guard Basics" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is an underhook important for the bottom player in half guard?
quiz.a: It prevents the top player from flattening the bottom player's shoulders to the mat, which is necessary for many passes and pins

Half Guard Basics looks simple when someone experienced does it -- and that is exactly why it deserves careful study. Half guard is a position where the bottom player controls one of the opponent's legs between both of their own, offering both defensive control and sweep or submission opportunities. In this lesson you will break the skill into learnable parts, practise each part slowly and deliberately, and then reassemble them into a smooth whole, which is how experienced practitioners in every field actually build their fluency.

A word on why this topic is taught the way it is. Research on skill acquisition consistently shows that people learn physical and procedural skills best in three phases: first understanding what correct execution looks like, then practising slowly with full attention to form, and finally adding speed, pressure, or complexity only after the basic pattern is stable. This lesson is organised around exactly that progression, so resist the temptation to skip ahead -- the order is doing real work.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: Half Guard Basics; Half guard is a position where the bottom player controls one of the opponent's legs between both of their own, offering both defensive control and sweep or submission opportunities. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Set up your workspace before beginning. The materials for this lesson are: gi or no-gi attire, training partner. Beyond the physical items, prepare the situation too: give yourself enough uninterrupted time to work through the steps slowly at least twice, choose a space where you can concentrate, and if the skill benefits from supervision or a partner, arrange that in advance. Professionals in every hands-on field treat setup as part of the skill itself, not a chore before the skill -- adopting that mindset early will serve you in every lesson that follows.

Here is the step-by-step method. As you work through it, narrate each step to yourself in your own words -- explaining as you go is one of the most reliable ways to move a procedure from short-term memory into lasting skill. Step 1: Trap one of the opponent's legs tightly between both of your own legs. There is no prize for hurrying this step -- accuracy first, then rhythm, then speed, in that order. Step 2: Establish an underhook on the near side to prevent them from flattening you out. Once this feels comfortable, try to notice what changed compared with your first attempt; that awareness is itself a skill and accelerates everything that follows. Step 3: Keep your head and shoulders active, avoiding lying flat on your back. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly. Step 4: Use frames and hip movement to prevent the top player from passing further. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing.

modules.title: Escaping and Sweeping from Half Guard
modules.description: From half guard, the bottom player can either sweep the opponent to reverse position or escape back to full guard, both relying on the underhook and leg control established earlier. This lesson covers common sweep and recovery options from half guard.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Escaping and Sweeping from Half Guard
From half guard, the bottom player can either sweep the opponent to reverse position or escape back to full guard, both relying on the underhook and leg control established earlier.
steps: From a strong half guard with an underhook, off-balance the opponent using the underhook and hip movement
Use your legs to elevate or trap the opponent's base leg while sweeping toward your underhook side
If a sweep isn't available, use frames and shrimping to free your trapped leg and recover full guard
Follow through to a dominant top position after a successful sweep
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Escaping and Sweeping from Half Guard" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

modules.title: Knee-on-Belly Position
modules.description: Knee-on-belly is a transitional pinning position where the top player places one knee on the opponent's stomach while posting the other leg out, offering mobility and pressure that can set up submissions or a mount transition. This lesson covers establishing and maintaining the position.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Knee-on-Belly Position

Knee-on-belly is a transitional pinning position where the top player places one knee on the opponent's stomach while posting the other leg out, offering mobility and pressure that can set up submissions or a mount transition.
steps: From side control, post one hand near the opponent's far shoulder and lift your hips slightly
Place one knee directly on the opponent's stomach, driving weight down through the shin
Post your other leg out to the side for base and mobility
Stay light and mobile, ready to shift to mount or back to side control as the opponent reacts
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Knee-on-Belly Position" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is knee-on-belly considered a mobile, transitional position rather than a static pin?
quiz.a: The posted leg allows the top player to quickly shift to mount, retreat to side control, or follow the opponent's movement, unlike a heavier static pin

modules.pro_tip: Knee-on-belly is intentionally uncomfortable for the opponent, which often causes a reaction you can exploit -- but always keep control safe and gradual.

modules.title: Rolling (Sparring) Etiquette and Tapping Out Safely
modules.description: Rolling, live sparring in BJJ, requires clear etiquette: tapping early and clearly, controlling submissions on training partners, and matching intensity appropriately to a partner's experience level. This lesson covers the safety culture that makes live training sustainable long-term.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Rolling (Sparring) Etiquette and Tapping Out Safely
Rolling, live sparring in BJJ, requires clear etiquette: tapping early and clearly, controlling submissions on training partners, and matching intensity appropriately to a partner's experience level.
steps: Tap clearly, by hand or voice, at the first sign of a submission taking effect -- don't wait to see if you can escape
Apply your own submissions slowly and release immediately when your partner taps
Match your intensity to your partner's experience and size, especially with beginners
Communicate injuries or discomfort before rolling, and stop immediately if something feels wrong
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Rolling (Sparring) Etiquette and Tapping Out Safely" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why should you tap at the first sign of a tight submission rather than waiting to see if you can escape?
quiz.a: Waiting too long risks a joint or blood choke injury; tapping early costs nothing but a reset, while waiting too long can cause real harm

modules.pro_tip: There's no shame in tapping often, especially as a beginner -- it's how you learn positions and survive to train another day.

modules.title: Self-Defense Applications of Jiu-Jitsu
modules.description: Beyond sport, BJJ techniques have practical self-defense applications, particularly for controlling an attacker on the ground and creating an opportunity to escape or call for help, and self-defense curricula emphasize these differently than sport-focused rolling. This lesson covers common standing grab defenses and ground control principles adapted for self-defense.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Self-Defense Applications of Jiu-Jitsu

Beyond sport, BJJ techniques have practical self-defense applications, particularly for controlling an attacker on the ground and creating an opportunity to escape or call for help, and self-defense curricula emphasize these differently than sport-focused rolling.
steps: Practice defending common grabs, such as a wrist grab or bear hug, using base and leverage rather than strength alone
Learn to use guard as a defensive position if taken to the ground, protecting yourself while creating distance
Practice standing back up safely using the technical stand-up while maintaining awareness of surroundings
Emphasize creating an opportunity to escape and seek help over prolonged engagement
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Self-Defense Applications of Jiu-Jitsu" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: How does a self-defense-focused BJJ lesson differ in goal from a sport-rolling session?
quiz.a: Self-defense emphasizes controlling a situation, escaping, and getting to safety, rather than scoring points or finishing a submission against a willing training partner

modules.pro_tip: In any real self-defense situation, prioritize escaping to safety and getting help over continuing to grapple, even if you have positional control.

modules.title: Building a Guard Passing Game Plan
modules.description: As practitioners advance, they begin to develop a personal guard passing game plan: a small set of complementary passes and follow-ups they can rely on against different types of guards, rather than trying to know every technique equally. learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Building a Guard Passing Game Plan

As practitioners advance, they begin to develop a personal guard passing game plan: a small set of complementary passes and follow-ups they can rely on against different types of guards, rather than trying to know every technique equally.
steps: Choose two or three passes that complement each other, such as a pressure pass and a speed pass

modules.title: Essential Safety Equipment
modules.description: Both sport fencing and HEMA require specific protective gear before any partner drilling or sparring, since even blunted or flexible practice weapons can cause injury without proper protection. This lesson introduces the core safety equipment required in a supervised class.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Essential Safety Equipment
Both sport fencing and HEMA require specific protective gear before any partner drilling or sparring, since even blunted or flexible practice weapons can cause injury without proper protection.
steps: Always wear a certified mask rated for the weapon and intensity of practice before any bladework begins
Wear a padded jacket (plastron) that covers the torso, and a fencing glove on the weapon hand
Use only practice weapons designed for sparring: blunted or flexible in fencing, blunt synthetic or steel HEMA feders in longsword
Inspect all equipment before each session for damage, such as a cracked mask mesh or a bent blade tip
materials_needed: practice weapon appropriate to the discipline
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Essential Safety Equipment" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why must equipment be inspected before every training session, not just occasionally?
quiz.a: Masks, jackets, and blades can develop hidden damage (mesh punctures, cracked seams, blade defects) that compromises their protection, so a quick pre-session check catches problems before an injury occurs

modules.pro_tip: Never spar or drill without full protective equipment, even for 'just a quick' exchange -- consistent safety habits prevent accidents.

modules.title: The Three Modern Fencing Weapons: Foil, Épée, and Sabre
modules.description: Olympic fencing includes three distinct weapons, each with different target areas and rules: foil targets the torso only with right-of-way rules, épée targets the entire body with no right-of-way, and sabre targets from the waist up including a cutting action, unlike the thrust-only foil and épée. This lesson introduces the differences between the three weapons.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Three Modern Fencing Weapons: Foil, Épée, and Sabre

Olympic fencing includes three distinct weapons, each with different target areas and rules: foil targets the torso only with right-of-way rules, épée targets the entire body with no right-of-way, and sabre targets from the waist up including a cutting action, unlike the thrust-only foil and épée.
steps: Learn that foil targets only the torso and uses right-of-way (priority) rules to determine who scores
Learn that épée targets the entire body, including the hands and feet, with no right-of-way -- simultaneous hits can both score
Learn that sabre targets the entire body above the waist and allows cutting touches, not just the thrusting point
Discuss how these differences shape each weapon's distinct strategy and footwork
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Three Modern Fencing Weapons: Foil, Épée, and Sabre" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Which fencing weapon has no right-of-way rule, meaning both fencers can score on a simultaneous hit?
quiz.a: Épée

modules.pro_tip: Choosing a weapon often comes down to trying all three, since each rewards a different style of movement and timing.

modules.title: The En Garde Stance
modules.description: The en garde stance is the foundational ready position in fencing, providing balance, mobility, and the ability to attack or defend quickly in any direction. This lesson covers the correct stance for footwork and bladework to follow.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The En Garde Stance
The en garde stance is the foundational ready position in fencing, providing balance, mobility, and the ability to attack or defend quickly in any direction.
steps: Stand with feet at a right angle, front foot pointing forward and back foot perpendicular to it
Bend both knees, keeping weight centered and balanced between both feet
Hold the weapon arm bent with the point/tip aimed at the target, and the rear arm raised for balance
Keep the back straight and head up, avoiding leaning forward or back
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The En Garde Stance" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is weight kept centered evenly between both feet in the en garde stance rather than favoring one leg?
quiz.a: Centered weight allows quick movement in any direction, forward, backward, or into a lunge, without first having to shift weight

modules.pro_tip: Practice holding en garde for extended periods to build the leg strength needed to move quickly from a low, stable stance.

modules.title: The Lunge
modules.description: The lunge is the primary attacking footwork in fencing, extending the weapon arm and front leg explosively to close distance and land a touch while keeping the option to recover back to en garde. This lesson covers the mechanics of an effective, balanced lunge.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Lunge
The lunge is the primary attacking footwork in fencing, extending the weapon arm and front leg explosively to close distance and land a touch while keeping the option to recover back to en garde.
steps: Extend the weapon arm first, aiming the point at the target
Push off the back leg and drive the front leg forward into a deep step, landing on the heel first
Keep the back leg straight and the back foot flat on the ground for stability
Recover back to the en garde position by pushing off the front leg
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Lunge" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does the weapon arm extend before the legs move in a proper lunge?

modules.pro_tip: Practice recovering from the lunge back to en garde just as much as the lunge itself; a fencer stuck in a lunge is vulnerable to a counter-attack.

modules.title: Basic Attacks and the Straight Thrust

learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Basic Attacks and the Straight Thrust
The straight thrust is the most fundamental fencing attack, extending the weapon directly toward the target in the most direct line available, typically combined with a lunge for reach.
steps: Identify an open target line where the opponent's blade isn't blocking your path

modules.title: Basic Parries and Ripostes
modules.description: A parry is a defensive blade action that deflects an opponent's attacking blade away from the target, and a riposte is the counter-attack that follows immediately after a successful parry. This lesson covers the fundamental parry positions and the parry-riposte sequence.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Basic Parries and Ripostes
A parry is a defensive blade action that deflects an opponent's attacking blade away from the target, and a riposte is the counter-attack that follows immediately after a successful parry.
steps: Recognize the incoming attack's line and select the corresponding parry to block it
Move the blade with a small, controlled motion to deflect the opponent's blade, rather than a large swinging block
Immediately riposte with a direct attack into the now-open target after the parry
Practice parry-riposte combinations slowly before increasing speed
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Basic Parries and Ripostes" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is a riposte, and when is it performed?
quiz.a: A riposte is a counter-attack performed immediately after successfully parrying (deflecting) an opponent's attack

modules.pro_tip: Keep parries small and efficient; a large, sweeping parry takes longer and can be more easily deceived or feinted around.

Effective longsword cuts generate power through proper body mechanics, hip rotation, and edge alignment, rather than arm strength alone, and understanding this mechanic is essential before any partnered cutting or sparring work.

modules.title: Footwork in Longsword: The Passing Step and Triangle Step
modules.description: Longsword footwork uses steps like the passing step (stepping one foot fully past the other) and triangular stepping patterns to control distance and angle while cutting or thrusting, differing from fencing's linear advance-retreat footwork. learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Footwork in Longsword: The Passing Step and Triangle Step

Longsword footwork uses steps like the passing step (stepping one foot fully past the other) and triangular stepping patterns to control distance and angle while cutting or thrusting, differing from fencing's linear advance-retreat footwork.
steps: Practice the passing step: stepping one foot fully past the other rather than sliding
Practice stepping off the centerline at an angle rather than only straight forward or back
Coordinate footwork timing with a cut, arriving at full extension as the foot lands
Drill combining passing steps with guard transitions
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Footwork in Longsword: The Passing Step and Triangle Step" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: How does the passing step in longsword footwork differ from the sliding advance used in modern sport fencing?
quiz.a: The passing step involves one foot stepping fully past the other foot, while a fencing advance slides the feet forward while maintaining the same relative foot order

modules.pro_tip: Practice footwork separately from cutting at first, then combine them once each feels natural on its own.

modules.title: Binding and Leverage Actions
modules.description: Binding occurs when two swords make contact and press against each other, and understanding leverage, using the strong part of your blade against the weak part of the opponent's, lets a fencer control or displace their opponent's blade safely. This lesson introduces the concept of binding and basic leverage principles.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Binding and Leverage Actions

Binding occurs when two swords make contact and press against each other, and understanding leverage, using the strong part of your blade against the weak part of the opponent's, lets a fencer control or displace their opponent's blade safely.
steps: Understand that a blade is divided into the strong (near the hilt) and weak (near the tip) sections
Practice binding, or pressing blades together, using your strong section against the opponent's weak section
Use the resulting leverage to control or redirect the opponent's blade
Practice recognizing when you have the advantageous bind and when you don't
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Binding and Leverage Actions" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does using the 'strong' part of your blade against the opponent's 'weak' part give you an advantage in a bind?
quiz.a: The section of the blade closer to the hilt has significantly more leverage than the section near the tip, so pressing your strong section against their weak section lets you control their blade more easily

modules.pro_tip: Feeling pressure through the bind (sometimes called 'feeling' in historical texts) tells you a great deal about an opponent's intention and strength.

modules.title: Distance and Timing (Tempo)
modules.description: Distance (measure) and timing (tempo) are core tactical concepts in both fencing and HEMA: controlling how far apart two fencers are, and recognizing the right moment to act, often matter more than raw speed or strength. learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Distance and Timing (Tempo)

Distance (measure) and timing (tempo) are core tactical concepts in both fencing and HEMA: controlling how far apart two fencers are, and recognizing the right moment to act, often matter more than raw speed or strength.
steps: Practice controlling distance so you can reach a target with a single step or lunge, but the opponent cannot easily reach you

modules.title: The Feint and Disengage
modules.description: A feint is a false attack meant to draw a defensive reaction, followed by a disengage, a small circular motion of the blade around the opponent's parry to open a new attacking line. This lesson covers using deception to open a target that's otherwise defended.

modules.title: The Beat Attack
modules.description: A beat is a sharp, controlled tap against the opponent's blade used to knock it aside momentarily, opening a line for an immediate attack, distinct from a parry because it's an offensive rather than purely defensive action. This lesson covers timing and executing a clean beat attack.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: The Beat Attack

A beat is a sharp, controlled tap against the opponent's blade used to knock it aside momentarily, opening a line for an immediate attack, distinct from a parry because it's an offensive rather than purely defensive action.
steps: Extend your blade toward the opponent's blade in the target line you intend to attack
Deliver a short, sharp tap against their blade, displacing it briefly
Immediately follow with a direct attack into the now-open line
Practice the timing so the beat and the follow-up attack flow as one continuous action
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "The Beat Attack" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: How does a beat attack differ from a parry, even though both involve contact with the opponent's blade?
quiz.a: A beat is an offensive action meant to open a line for your own attack, while a parry is a defensive action meant to block an opponent's incoming attack

modules.pro_tip: A beat should be sharp and brief -- lingering contact gives the opponent time to react and re-close the line.

modules.title: Rapier Basics (Historical Context)

steps: Understand the rapier's design: long, primarily thrust-oriented, with a complex hilt for hand protection

quiz.q: What is one defensive role an off-hand dagger or buckler plays in historical sword-and-companion-weapon systems?

modules.title: Épée Tactics: The Whole-Body Target

steps: Study a treatise illustration alongside its accompanying text description

modules.title: Advanced Compound Actions and Second-Intention Attacks
modules.description: A second-intention attack is a deliberately incomplete or vulnerable-looking first action designed specifically to draw a predictable counter-attack, which the fencer is already prepared to parry and riposte. This advanced tactical layer requires strong fundamentals in feints, parries, and timing. This lesson introduces the concept.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Advanced Compound Actions and Second-Intention Attacks

A second-intention attack is a deliberately incomplete or vulnerable-looking first action designed specifically to draw a predictable counter-attack, which the fencer is already prepared to parry and riposte.
steps: Launch a deliberately exploitable first attack, anticipating a specific counter-attack in response
Prepare and execute a parry against the anticipated counter
Follow immediately with a riposte into the newly opened target
Discuss why this tactic requires reading an opponent's typical tendencies to work reliably
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Advanced Compound Actions and Second-Intention Attacks" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a simple feint and a second-intention attack?
quiz.a: A feint is meant to draw a defensive parry that opens a line for a follow-up attack, while a second-intention attack deliberately invites the opponent's own counter-attack, which the fencer is prepared to parry and riposte

modules.pro_tip: Second-intention tactics work best against opponents whose tendencies you've observed -- they rely on prediction as much as execution.

modules.title: Injury Prevention and Recognizing Overtraining

modules.title: Warm-Up and Cool-Down Routines
modules.description: A proper warm-up prepares the joints, muscles, and reflexes for the explosive, repetitive movements of sword training, while a cool-down supports recovery, and skipping either increases injury risk over time. This lesson covers structuring an effective warm-up and cool-down.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Warm-Up and Cool-Down Routines

A proper warm-up prepares the joints, muscles, and reflexes for the explosive, repetitive movements of sword training, while a cool-down supports recovery, and skipping either increases injury risk over time.
steps: Begin with light cardio to raise heart rate and body temperature gradually
Perform dynamic stretches and joint mobility drills targeting the shoulders, wrists, hips, and knees
Include footwork-specific movement drills as part of the warm-up before picking up a weapon
Finish training sessions with light static stretching and a brief cool-down walk
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Warm-Up and Cool-Down Routines" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why are dynamic stretches generally preferred over static stretches during a warm-up, before training?
quiz.a: Dynamic stretches actively move the joints through range of motion and raise body temperature, better preparing muscles for explosive movement than static stretches, which are better suited to cool-down

modules.title: The Hook

learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Basic Counter-Punching
Counter-punching responds to an opponent's committed punch with an immediate, well-timed strike, requiring solid defensive skills, slipping, blocking, or parrying, as a foundation.
steps: Have a partner throw a slow, telegraphed jab
Defend using a slip, block, or parry as appropriate
Immediately counter with a punch into the resulting opening
Practice slowly, increasing speed only as timing becomes consistent
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Basic Counter-Punching" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is counter-punching typically taught only after basic offense and defense are both solid on their own?
quiz.a: Effective countering depends on a reliable defensive action first, since a rushed or unreliable defense leaves no safe foundation to build a counter-punch from

modules.lesson_text:
This lesson covers Basic Counter-Punching in depth. Counter-punching responds to an opponent's committed punch with an immediate, well-timed strike, requiring solid defensive skills, slipping, blocking, or parrying, as a foundation. It is typically introduced once basic offense and defense are both comfortable. Rather than treating it as a trick to memorise, the goal here is genuine competence: understanding the reasoning behind each step well enough that you could explain it to someone else, adapt it when conditions change, and recognise when something is going wrong early enough to correct it.

It is worth pausing on why this lesson matters before diving in. Competence at a practical skill is not just about the skill itself; it changes how you approach unfamiliar problems generally. When you have genuinely mastered even one hands-on skill -- taken it from clumsy first attempts to smooth, reliable execution -- you know from experience that difficulty is temporary and that methodical practice works. That confidence, built on real evidence rather than positive thinking, is one of the most valuable things any learner can own, and every lesson in this pathway is another chance to reinforce it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to: Understand and safely practice: Basic Counter-Punching; Counter-punching responds to an opponent's committed punch with an immediate, well-timed strike, requiring solid defensive skills, slipping, blocking, or parrying, as a foundation. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Vague familiarity is the great impostor of learning; demonstrable ability is the real thing.

Preparation comes first. For this lesson you will want: Partner, Focus mitts. Lay everything out before you start rather than fetching things mid-task; interruptions are where beginners lose focus and where avoidable mistakes creep in. Check the condition of what you are using -- worn, damaged, or makeshift equipment makes every step harder and can make some steps unsafe. If you are missing something, it is almost always better to postpone the practice session than to improvise with a poor substitute while you are still learning what 'correct' feels like.

The heart of the lesson is the following sequence. Read all the steps once before performing any of them, so you know where each one is heading. Step 1: Have a partner throw a slow, telegraphed jab. Once this feels comfortable, try to notice what changed compared with your first attempt; that awareness is itself a skill and accelerates everything that follows. Step 2: Defend using a slip, block, or parry as appropriate. Do this deliberately and check the result before moving on -- each step in the sequence assumes the previous one was done correctly. Step 3: Immediately counter with a punch into the resulting opening. If this step feels awkward at first, that is normal; repeat it in isolation a few times until it smooths out before continuing. Step 4: Practice slowly, increasing speed only as timing becomes consistent. Pay particular attention here, because this is a step where small errors tend to compound later in the sequence.

Beginners tend to make the same handful of mistakes with skills like this, and knowing them in advance helps you catch them early. The first is rushing: performing the motions of the steps without the attention that makes them stick, which produces the appearance of practice without the benefit. The second is skipping preparation, which quietly raises the difficulty of everything downstream. The third is practising errors -- repeating a step incorrectly until the wrong version becomes the habit, which then takes far longer to unlearn than it would have taken to learn correctly. If you notice any of these patterns in yourself, stop, slow down, and rebuild the step from its correct form.

Keep the safety guidance in mind throughout: Focus on making the defensive action reliable first; the counter-punch itself often becomes the easier half of the skill. This is not boilerplate -- the caution exists because the risk it names is the one most often realised when people are careless with this material. Good practitioners are not the ones who never think about risk; they are the ones who manage it so habitually that it looks effortless.

For practice, start here: Practice "Basic Counter-Punching" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed. Treat that as a template you can repeat and extend. A useful structure is short, frequent sessions -- fifteen to twenty focused minutes several times a week will outperform a single long weekend session, because skills consolidate between practices, not just during them. Keep a simple log of what you practised and what felt difficult; over a few weeks the log becomes a map of your progress and tells you exactly what to work on next.

Check your understanding before moving on. Consider this question: Why is counter-punching typically taught only after basic offense and defense are both solid on their own? The answer -- Effective countering depends on a reliable defensive action first, since a rushed or unreliable defense leaves no safe foundation to build a counter-punch from -- is worth actually reasoning through rather than just reading, because the reasoning is what you will rely on when a real situation doesn't look exactly like the practice one.

Once the basic sequence is reliable, progress it deliberately. First add consistency: can you perform the skill correctly five times in a row? Then add mild pressure: time constraints, an observer, or slightly less ideal conditions. Then add variation: change the context enough that you must adapt rather than replay a memorised script. This staged progression -- reliability, pressure, variation -- is how training programmes in everything from medicine to sport build skills that hold up in the real world, and it applies just as well here.

Remember where this sits in the wider Boxing pathway: the lessons before it built the context this one relies on, and the lessons after it will assume the ability you are building now. If any prerequisite feels shaky, a quick review before the next session is cheap insurance.

Finally, connect this lesson to the bigger picture. No single skill stands alone: this one links naturally to its neighbours in the pathway, and fluency here will make several later lessons noticeably easier. Come back to this material after a few weeks of practice -- returning to fundamentals with experienced eyes is something every advanced practitioner does, and each pass reveals detail that was invisible the first time. Mastery is not a destination you arrive at once; it is the compounding result of exactly the kind of careful, honest practice this lesson has laid out.

modules.title: Slip-and-Counter: Jab
modules.description: This drill combines slipping an incoming jab with an immediate counter, typically a cross, building the specific timing connection between a defensive slip and an offensive response. It's a foundational counter-punching combination.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Slip-and-Counter: Jab
This drill combines slipping an incoming jab with an immediate counter, typically a cross, building the specific timing connection between a defensive slip and an offensive response.
steps: Have a partner throw a slow, telegraphed jab
Slip slightly off the centerline to avoid the punch
Immediately counter with a cross from the slipped position
Gradually increase the jab's speed only as timing becomes reliable
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Slip-and-Counter: Jab" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why does slipping a jab create a good opportunity for a cross counter specifically?
quiz.a: Slipping moves the head off-line while keeping the body positioned to rotate into a cross, so the counter can be thrown immediately from a naturally loaded position

modules.pro_tip: Drill this slip-and-counter combination slowly at first, since rushing the timing often results in getting hit rather than slipping successfully.

modules.title: Body Punching
modules.description: Punching to the body, particularly with hooks and uppercuts targeting the ribs and midsection, is an often underemphasized skill that can affect an opponent's stamina and guard over the course of a match. This lesson introduces deliberate body-targeting technique.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Body Punching

Punching to the body, particularly with hooks and uppercuts targeting the ribs and midsection, is an often underemphasized skill that can affect an opponent's stamina and guard over the course of a match.
steps: Practice bending the knees slightly to lower punching level to the body
Throw hooks and uppercuts targeting the ribs and midsection on a heavy bag
Maintain guard while lowering level for a body punch
Discuss why body punching can affect an opponent later in a match, not just immediately
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Body Punching" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why might body punching be tactically valuable even if it doesn't land as a dramatic single strike?
quiz.a: Consistent body punching can wear down an opponent's stamina and lower their guard over the course of a match, creating cumulative effects beyond any single punch's immediate impact

modules.pro_tip: Practice lowering your level with the knees for body punches, rather than bending forward from the waist, which exposes the head.

modules.title: Combination Building: Three- and Four-Punch Combos
modules.description: Building longer combinations, such as jab-cross-hook-cross, develops the ability to chain multiple punch types fluidly while maintaining balance and guard throughout the sequence. These combinations are typically drilled extensively on pads and bags.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Combination Building: Three- and Four-Punch Combos
Building longer combinations, such as jab-cross-hook-cross, develops the ability to chain multiple punch types fluidly while maintaining balance and guard throughout the sequence.
steps: Learn a specific three- or four-punch combination taught by your instructor
Drill the combination slowly, focusing on correct form for each punch
Gradually increase speed while maintaining balance and guard
Practice resetting to guard cleanly after the full combination
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Combination Building: Three- and Four-Punch Combos" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why are longer punch combinations typically drilled extensively on pads or bags before being used in sparring?
quiz.a: Pad and bag work let a boxer build the timing, balance, and muscle memory for a longer sequence in a controlled setting before adding the unpredictability of a live opponent

modules.pro_tip: Break a long combination into smaller two-punch chunks if it feels rushed, then link the chunks together gradually.

modules.title: Angles and Pivoting
modules.description: Moving at an angle relative to an opponent, rather than straight forward or backward, creates openings and avoids a predictable, straight-line exchange. Pivoting on the lead foot is a key technique for changing angle efficiently.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Angles and Pivoting
Moving at an angle relative to an opponent, rather than straight forward or backward, creates openings and avoids a predictable, straight-line exchange.
steps: Practice pivoting on the lead foot to change angle relative to a partner
Combine an angle change with a follow-up jab or combination
Discuss why straight-line movement is more predictable and easier to time
Practice creating an angle after slipping a punch
modules.hands_on_activity: Practice "Angles and Pivoting" slowly and safely, focusing on correct form before speed.

quiz.q: Why is moving at an angle generally considered more effective than moving straight backward or forward?
quiz.a: Straight-line movement is easier for an opponent to predict and time, while angular movement creates new openings and disrupts an opponent's ability to line up their own punches

modules.pro_tip: Practice pivoting and creating angles specifically after a slip, since the two skills combine naturally into an effective defensive-to-offensive sequence.

modules.title: Clinching and Breaking Cleanly
modules.description: Clinching, a brief close-range hold, can occur when boxers get too close, and knowing how to break cleanly and safely from a clinch, following referee instruction in competition, is a practical skill. This is taught with an emphasis on safety and proper etiquette.
learning_objectives: Understand and safely practice: Clinching and Breaking Cleanly

Skills like this one compound: each hour of correct, focused practice makes the next hour more productive, and the habits you build here -- preparing properly, working in the right order, checking your results -- transfer directly to every other skill in this pathway. Keep these objectives visible as you work -- they are the measuring stick for whether the practice is working, and each one is phrased as something you can actually demonstrate rather than something you vaguely feel familiar with. Lay everything out before you start rather than fetching things mid-task; interruptions are where beginners lose focus and where avoidable mistakes creep in.
